The United States, China, and India were the most productive countries, while a core group of highly connected authors shaped collaborative structures. Keyword clustering revealed a clear thematic progression from algorithmic development and image segmentation toward diagnostic imaging applications, digital dentistry integration, and workflow optimisation. Among the 75 systematic reviews evaluated using ROBIS, 50 (66.7%) demonstrated an unclear overall risk of bias, 24 (32.0%) showed a low risk of bias, and only one (1.3%) was classified as high risk, indicating that methodological transparency and evidence synthesis have not progressed at the same pace as technological innovation.

Conclusion

AI research in dentistry is experiencing rapid expansion and increasing international collaboration, and continuous thematic evolution towards clinically relevant applications. However, the ROBIS assessment indicates that improvements in methodological quality and reporting transparency of evidence syntheses are still required to strengthen confidence in the current evidence base. Future studies should prioritise multicentre validation, standardised evaluation frameworks, rigorous systematic reviews, and clinically meaningful outcome measures to facilitate the safe and effective translation of AI into routine dental practice.

records.title: Artificial intelligence applications in long-term care facilities: a scoping review across planning, design, operation, and assessment.

content.title: Artificial intelligence applications in long-term care facilities: a scoping review across planning, design, operation, and assessment.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Improving the quality of long-term care facilities (LTCFs) is critical to safeguarding the health, safety, dignity, and quality of life of older adults amid global population aging. However, traditional design methods for LTCFs rely heavily on static codes and empirical judgment, limiting their ability to respond to dynamic care needs and balance multiple objectives across lifecycle stages. To address these limitations, artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising solution through dynamic optimization and intelligent decision-making.

Methods

A scoping review was conducted to systematically map the applications of AI in LTCFs across four lifecycle stages: planning and site selection, architectural design, operation and management, and assessment and retrofit. Searches were performed in Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, SAGE Journals, and CNKI for literature published between January 2010 and December 2025, resulting in the inclusion of 38 eligible publications. The review was guided by the methodological framework proposed by Arksey and O'Malley and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR.

Results

Four main application pathways were identified, including prediction and evaluation, generation and evolution, sensing and recognition, and simulation and modeling. Specifically, AI was applied to site-selection evaluation and demand forecasting during planning; spatial layout generation and intelligent equipment integration during design; safety monitoring, behavior recognition, and environmental control during operation; and comfort and safety assessment and retrofit optimization during assessment. Research was concentrated in operation and management, whereas evidence on assessment and retrofit remained limited.

Discussion

Overall, AI shows potential to shift LTCFs from static, fragmented, and experience-based practices toward more data-informed, adaptive, and person-centered care environments. However, implementation remains constrained by data quality and standardization, facility heterogeneity, system integration, equitable access, privacy, and ethical concerns. This review provides planners, architects, engineers, care providers, facility managers, and public health decision-makers with a technology roadmap and identifies priorities for using AI-enabled built environments to support high-quality older adult care and sustainable long-term care systems.

records.title: Glycemic dysregulation and insulin resistance across acute and post-acute COVID-19: a systematic review and meta-analysis of etiologic and prognostic evidence.

content.title: Glycemic dysregulation and insulin resistance across acute and post-acute COVID-19: a systematic review and meta-analysis of etiologic and prognostic evidence.
content.abstract:
Background

Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) can disrupt glucose regulation through inflammation, adipose-tissue dysfunction, impaired insulin signaling, and variable β-cell compensation. These evidence domains remain incompletely integrated.

Objective

To synthesize evidence on glycemic dysregulation and insulin resistance or insulin sensitivity across acute and post-acute COVID-19, including metabolic trajectories and associations with adverse clinical outcomes.

Methods

PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect were searched. Eligible studies evaluated glucose regulation and at least one insulin-resistance or insulin-sensitivity measure during or after COVID-19. Etiological and prognostic evidence was analyzed as related but distinct domains. Prognostic meta-analysis evaluated study-defined acute hyperglycemic phenotypes; insulin-resistance or insulin-sensitivity assessment was a study-level eligibility criterion rather than part of a participant-level composite exposure. Unadjusted risk ratios (RRs) from event counts were pooled using restricted maximum-likelihood random-effects models with Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Non-combinable evidence was synthesized according to Synthesis Without Meta-analysis principles. Risk of bias was assessed using design-appropriate tools, and certainty was evaluated with GRADE. The protocol and analytical plan were retrospectively registered in OSF on August 21, 2026 (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/K5FWU).

Results

Twenty independent studies represented by 23 reports. Acute hyperglycemic phenotypes were associated with increased short-term all-cause mortality (four studies; 1,079 participants; RR 2.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.21-3.64; I2=31.3%; 95% prediction interval 0.96-4.56) and invasive mechanical ventilation (three studies; 679 participants; RR 3.64, 95% CI 1.74-7.61; I2=0%). Mortality estimates remained directionally stable in sensitivity analysis. Adding a large study using peak in-hospital glucose preserved the mortality association but produced substantial heterogeneity for ventilation. Etiological evidence showed no uniform post-COVID trajectory: insulin resistance or glycemic abnormalities resolved in some populations, persisted in others, and progressed toward newly diagnosed diabetes in a subset. Mechanistic evidence implicated inflammatory stress, adipose-tissue dysfunction, impaired insulin signaling, and variable β-cell responses.

Conclusions

Study-defined acute hyperglycemic phenotypes were associated with adverse COVID-19 outcomes in studies that also assessed insulin resistance or insulin sensitivity. These unadjusted estimates should not be interpreted as effects of a combined phenotype or as causal associations. Persistent metabolic abnormalities occurred heterogeneously, supporting standardized participant-level definitions and controlled longitudinal studies.

Systematic review registration

https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/K5FWU, identifier 10.17605/OSF.IO/K5FWU.

records.title: Art-based interventions and social-emotional outcomes in children with autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis with a proposed neurodevelopmental framework.

content.title: Art-based interventions and social-emotional outcomes in children with autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis with a proposed neurodevelopmental framework.
content.abstract: Emotional intelligence (EI)-related social-emotional difficulties in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are linked to atypical social-brain development, including altered amygdala-prefrontal, fusiform, and frontoparietal function during affective processing. This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified the effects of visual art-based interventions on EI and EI-related social-emotional outcomes in children with ASD, and integrated convergent neuroimaging evidence into a testable neurodevelopmental framework. Following PRISMA 2020, PubMed, Web of Science, PsycINFO, the Cochrane Library, ProQuest Dissertations, ClinicalTrials.gov, and gray literature were searched from inception to 31 December 2025, with an updated search on 15 May 2026 and a supplementary public-source update on 17 August 2026. Eligible studies included controlled, quasi-experimental, or pre-post visual art-based interventions lasting at least 4 weeks in children aged 3-18 years with clinically diagnosed ASD. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2.0 and ROBINS-I, and Hedges' g was pooled using random-effects models. Fourteen studies involving 521 participants aged 3-15 years across seven countries were included; 481 participants were children with autism spectrum disorder and 40 were typically developing comparison participants. Twelve studies used a control group and formed the basis of the primary analysis. Art-based interventions were associated with a small-to-moderate improvement in EI-related social-emotional outcomes (all studies: k = 14, SMD = 0.47, 95% CI [0.30, 0.63], p < 0.001; controlled studies only: k = 12, SMD = 0.46, 95% CI [0.28, 0.64]), with no detectable statistical heterogeneity [I 2 = 0, 95% prediction interval (0.28, 0.65)]. Exploratory subgroup analyses showed no material difference between multimodal and drawing-focused programs (p = 0.79) and a larger point estimate for interventions lasting 9-16 weeks, but these moderator findings were descriptive and should be interpreted cautiously. Under the GRADE approach the certainty of the evidence was rated low. Neuroimaging evidence suggests that visual art engagement may support EI through frontoparietal attentional control, graded affective exposure, and prefrontal regulation of limbic reactivity. Direct longitudinal neuroimaging trials are needed to test these proposed mechanisms.

records.title: Legal and Regulatory Considerations for Artificial Intelligence Use in Medical and Radiology Research.
records.publisher: The Indian journal of radiology & imaging

content.title: Legal and Regulatory Considerations for Artificial Intelligence Use in Medical and Radiology Research.
content.abstract:
Background

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into medical imaging and radiology research, improving image acquisition, interpretation, workflow efficiency, and decision support. However, its rapid adoption has introduced complex legal and regulatory challenges involving patient privacy, data governance, algorithm validation, liability, intellectual property, transparency, cybersecurity, and ethical oversight. A comprehensive understanding of the evolving legal landscape is essential for the safe, effective, and legally compliant implementation of AI in radiology.

Methods

A narrative review of the published literature and current regulatory guidance was conducted. Relevant international legal and regulatory frameworks governing AI in medical imaging were evaluated, including the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, General Data Protection Regulation, U.S. Food and Drug Administration guidance on Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, World Health Organization recommendations, International Medical Device Regulators Forum principles, and selected national regulations. Key topics reviewed included data protection, informed consent, AI validation, regulatory approval pathways, post-market surveillance, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, explainability, and medico-legal responsibility.

Results

Current regulatory frameworks increasingly classify AI-enabled radiology software as SaMD, requiring risk-based evaluation, clinical validation, quality management systems, and continuous post-market performance monitoring. Regulatory authorities emphasize transparency, human oversight, data security, and lifecycle governance of AI systems. Nevertheless, important legal challenges remain, including liability for AI-assisted diagnostic errors, ownership of AI-generated outputs, secondary use of imaging data, cross-border data sharing, algorithmic bias, and regulation of adaptive or continuously learning AI models.

Conclusions

The legal framework governing AI in radiology is evolving in parallel with technological innovation. Responsible integration of AI into clinical practice and research requires harmonized international regulations, robust data governance, standardized validation protocols, transparent algorithm development, and clearly defined legal accountability. Continued collaboration among radiologists, researchers, regulators, policymakers, industry, and legal experts will be essential to ensure that AI technologies remain safe, ethical, equitable, and trustworthy while maximizing their potential to improve patient care.

records.title: A Meta-synthesis of nursing students' experiences with generative artificial intelligence-assisted learning.

content.title: A Meta-synthesis of nursing students' experiences with generative artificial intelligence-assisted learning.
content.abstract:
Objective

To systematically evaluate the real experiences of nursing students participating in generative artificial intelligence-assisted learning.

Methods

Electronic searches were conducted in the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), VIP Database, Scopus, Wanfang Data, and the China Biomedical Literature Database (CBM), Web of Science, PubMed, Cochrane, Embase, and CINAHL databases for qualitative studies on the experiences of nursing students with generative AI-assisted learning from the establishment of the databases to March 2026. Qualitative studies on nursing students' experiences with generative AI-assisted learning were screened, appraised, and synthesized using thematic synthesis.

Results

Eighteen studies were included in the synthesis. A total of 49 themes were identified and organized into 13 categories, leading to four integrated findings: (1) dual experience of empowerment and challenges, (2) internal conflict between technology and nursing humanism, (3) user experience differentiation amid Practical Constraints, (4) general demand for supporting systems and educational reform.

Conclusion

This study found that nursing students' experiences with generative AI are shaped by both the opportunities and challenges associated with its use in learning. These findings highlight the need for nursing educators to strengthen students' AI literacy, critical thinking, and ethical awareness, for curriculum designers to integrate AI-related competencies into nursing curricula while maintaining a strong emphasis on humanistic care, and for policymakers to establish clear governance frameworks and educational guidelines to support the responsible use of AI in nursing education.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261367837, identifier CRD420261367837.

records.title: Artificial intelligence for binary dental caries diagnosis using intraoral images and dental radiographs: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Artificial intelligence for binary dental caries diagnosis using intraoral images and dental radiographs: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objectives

Artificial intelligence (AI) has shown increasing potential in dental diagnostics, yet its accuracy for binary classification of dental caries across different imaging modalities remains unclear. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the diagnostic performance of AI models using clinical intraoral images and dental radiographs.

Methods

Following the PRISMA-DTA guidelines, PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore were systematically searched for studies published between January 2015 and June 2025. Eligible studies applied AI models for caries diagnosis with extractable sensitivity and specificity. Data on dentition, dataset, analysis unit, caries prevalence in test dataset, and preprocessing methods were extracted. Reporting quality and risk of bias were assessed using CLAIM and QUADAS-2. Pooled estimates were calculated with a bivariate random-effects model, with subgroup analyses by image type and analytical unit.

Results

25 studies met the criteria, and 13 were included in the meta-analysis. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the curve (AUC) were 0.86, 0.91 and 0.94, respectively. Intraoral image-based models achieved higher sensitivity (0.88) and AUC (0.95), while radiograph-based models showed higher specificity (0.92). Tooth-level analyses yielded stable, clinically relevant performance (0.87/0.91). High heterogeneity (I² > 90%) was partly explained by image type, model architecture, reference standard variation, and test set caries prevalence.

Conclusion

AI models showed good diagnostic accuracy for caries detection across imaging modalities and analytical units. However, given the substantial heterogeneity and limitations in study quality and reference standards, these summary estimates should be interpreted with caution. AI-based systems may serve as complementary decision-support tools in clinical practice, but further standardization, external validation, and high-quality multicenter studies are required before broad clinical implementation.

records.title: Music-based interventions for acute and short-term anxiety in nursing students: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Music-based interventions for acute and short-term anxiety in nursing students: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Nursing students encounter acute anxiety during examinations, simulations, clinical skills training, and other health-related student contexts. We evaluated music-based interventions, with acute or short-term self-reported anxiety as the principal outcome and other psychological, physiological, health, and educational outcomes as secondary domains.

Methods

Following peer review, we repeated searches in PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL Complete, Embase, APA PsycINFO, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), the Web of Science Core Collection, and ClinicalTrials.gov from their inception to 19 September 2026, without outcome, study design, publication type, or language limits. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted, and assessed the risk of bias. The principal meta-analysis used a uniform post-intervention Hedges' g from each eligible, individually randomized parallel-group trial. Random-effects models were estimated using Restricted Maximum Likelihood or Residual Maximum Likelihood (REML); Wald confidence intervals were the primary estimate, and Hartung-Knapp and prediction intervals were used to assess small-sample uncertainty.

Results

Of the 737 records identified, 337 duplicates were removed, and 400 records were screened. A total of 64 reports were sought; 39 unique complete documents were assessed; 26 reports representing 24 studies were included; and 13 full-text reports were excluded. Twenty studies were randomized, and four were non-randomized. Nine parallel-group trials (650 participants) contributed to the principal anxiety synthesis (g = -0.31, 95% confidence interval (CI): -0.58 to -0.04; p = 0.024; I 2 = 64%; τ 2 = 0.107). The Hartung-Knapp interval (from -0.63 to 0.01; p = 0.055) and the 95% prediction interval (from -1.15 to 0.53) crossed zero. All nine principal trials were at high overall risk of bias, and certainty was very low.

Conclusion

Music-based interventions may reduce acute or short-term self-reported anxiety on average. However, the results are sensitive to the method used to quantify uncertainty, and the effects are likely to vary across settings. Evidence is insufficient to infer sustained psychological benefits, improved learning, or support for routine implementation.

Systematic review registration

The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251274752). Public record URL: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251274752.

records.title: Deep learning for diagnostic and clinical decision support in companion animals: a systematic review of CNN- and LSTM-based approaches.

content.title: Deep learning for diagnostic and clinical decision support in companion animals: a systematic review of CNN- and LSTM-based approaches.
content.abstract: Early disease detection prior to the onset of advanced clinical signs remains a critical imperative in veterinary medicine. This systematic review provides a methodological synthesis of Convolutional Neural Networks and Long Short-Term Memory networks applied to diagnostic and clinical decision support in canine and feline patients, evaluating both algorithmic performance and clinical feasibility. Adhering to the PICO-CS framework and PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we queried Scopus and Web of Science for peer-reviewed studies published between 2021 and 2026, retrieving a final corpus of 57 primary studies. Eleven clinical domains were identified, with evidence heavily concentrated in Oncology (28.1%), Cardiology (15.8%), and Pulmonology (12.3%). CNN architectures predominated in spatial imaging modalities-including radiographs, clinical photography, ultrasonography, and microscopic imagery-whereas LSTM networks were deployed for temporal signals and sensor-derived telemetry. Binary classification tasks achieved the highest performance metrics (accuracy reaching up to 99%), whereas multi-class formulations exhibited broader variability due to dataset imbalance. Cross-study benchmarking revealed substantial heterogeneity in datasets, evaluation metrics, and validation protocols, while reliance on high-performance computational infrastructure poses a barrier to point-of-care deployment in resource-constrained clinics. We conclude that while deep learning architectures hold significant promise as clinical decision-support tools, transitioning to routine veterinary practice requires prospective external validation, representative open-access datasets, and lightweight models optimized for conventional clinical hardware.

records.title: Machine learning-based assessment of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in breast cancer histopathology: a systematic review and evidence-gap analysis of translational readiness.

content.title: Machine learning-based assessment of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in breast cancer histopathology: a systematic review and evidence-gap analysis of translational readiness.
content.abstract:
Background

Machine learning-based assessment of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) has been proposed to improve the reproducibility and clinical utility of immune-contexture evaluation in breast cancer histopathology. However, existing studies differ substantially in task definition, annotation strategy, model architecture, validation design, and clinical endpoint. This systematic review and evidence-gap analysis aimed to map the translational readiness of TIL-related machine learning studies in breast cancer histopathology and to identify cluster-specific methodological gaps.

Methods

A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar was conducted up to 20 April 2026, supplemented by backward citation tracing and a targeted Google search of the 30 most relevant additional results. Eligible studies included breast cancer histopathology-based machine learning, deep learning, artificial intelligence, or computational image-analysis studies evaluating TILs or TIL-related immune-cell features. Studies were grouped by principal application into detection/classification, outcome prognostication, and treatment-response prediction. Extracted variables included data source, specimen type, model family, annotation strategy, validation design, clinical comparator use, calibration, decision-curve analysis, incremental value, reproducibility, and methodological challenges. Because of heterogeneity in endpoints and performance metrics, synthesis was descriptive and evidence-map based.

Results

The primary evidence map included 51 histopathology-image studies: 19 detection/classification, 18 outcome prognostication, and 14 treatment-response prediction studies. External validation was reported in 31.6% of detection/classification studies, 61.1% of prognostication studies, and 57.1% of treatment-response prediction studies. Clinical comparator reporting increased across the same continuum, from 63.2% to 94.4% and 92.9%, respectively. However, calibration was reported in only one prognostication study (5.6%) and in no detection/classification or treatment-response prediction studies. Decision-curve analysis was similarly limited to one prognostication study. Class imbalance was near-universal (94.7-100% across clusters). Scanner/stain robustness was addressed in a majority of studies (63.2-83.3%), but fairness or subgroup analyses remained inconsistently reported (27.8-57.1%).

Conclusions

TIL machine learning in breast cancer is technically active but clinically under-validated. Future studies should move beyond model development toward externally validated, calibrated, clinically benchmarked, reproducible, and decision-relevant evidence, using cluster-specific planning standards for detection, prognostication, and treatment-response prediction.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024574566, identifier CRD42024574566.

records.title: Use of artificial intelligence for detection of MB2 canals in maxillary first molars on CBCT: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Use of artificial intelligence for detection of MB2 canals in maxillary first molars on CBCT: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Detecting the second mesiobuccal (MB2) canal in maxillary first molars is challenging, even with cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). Artificial intelligence (AI), especially deep learning, has been explored as a tool to aid detection.

Objectives

This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of AI in identifying MB2 canals on CBCT.

Methods

Following PRISMA guidelines, a comprehensive electronic search across five databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Scopus Secondary) retrieved 52 articles. After removing duplicates and screening titles/abstracts, 7 full texts were assessed, of which 4 met the inclusion criteria. Studies were eligible if they applied AI algorithms for MB2 detection in CBCT images and reported diagnostic performance outcomes. Data extraction included study design, dataset size, AI model architecture, and diagnostic metrics. Pooled estimates of sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were calculated using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed with the I² statistic, and publication bias was evaluated with Egger's test.

Results

Four studies were included. AI models achieved a pooled sensitivity of 0.82 and specificity of 0.74. Deep learning models outperformed traditional machine learning, with higher sensitivity (0.87 vs. 0.80), specificity (0.90 vs. 0.68), and accuracy (0.84 vs. 0.75). Considerable heterogeneity and small sample sizes limited generalizability.

Conclusion

AI, particularly deep learning, shows promise in detecting MB2 canals on CBCT. While current evidence is preliminary, standardised AI training and reporting protocols, together with larger multicenter studies, are needed to validate these tools. Clinically, AI could serve as a supplementary aid to improve diagnostic consistency and reduce missed canals during endodontic treatment.

records.title: Parkinson's disease diagnosis using machine learning and multimodal biomarkers: A systematic review.

content.title: Parkinson's disease diagnosis using machine learning and multimodal biomarkers: A systematic review.
content.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder and the fastest-growing neurological condition globally, with an estimated 10.5 million people living with PD in 2026 and projections exceeding 14.2 million by 2040 according to the World Health Organization. Despite this staggering burden, diagnosis continues to depend on clinical motor signs that appear only after 60%-80% of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra have been irreversibly lost, and specialist misdiagnosis rates reach 25% at early disease stages even in dedicated movement disorder centers. This systematic review synthesizes evidence from 239 studies drawn from 5847 screened records (2016-2026), critically evaluating unimodal diagnostic approaches encompassing dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography (DAT-SPECT), quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), alpha-synuclein (α-syn) seed amplification assay (SAA), neurofilament light chain (NfL), genetic risk markers, voice and speech biomarkers, gait and movement metrics, electroencephalography (EEG), and handwriting analysis, alongside their integration into multimodal machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) frameworks with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) components. Across 87 quantitative studies, the α-syn SAA achieved a sensitivity of 84%-92% and specificity of 93%-98% in prodromal cohorts. DAT-SPECT achieved a pooled sensitivity and specificity of approximately 90% but could not differentiate PD from atypical parkinsonian syndromes (APS). Multimodal fusion architectures, particularly cross-attention transformers integrating motor, voice, and gait data, consistently outperformed unimodal approaches by 4%-8% in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with the largest gains in early stage detection and differential diagnosis tasks. XAI methods, including SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM), and integrated gradients, were reported in only 31% of deep learning studies. This indicates a transparency gap with direct regulatory consequences. Across all modalities, only 22% of studies reported external validation, and multicenter prospective evidence remains scarce. These two deficits, rather than model architecture, are now the principal barriers to clinical adoption. This review provides an actionable roadmap for researchers, clinicians, and regulatory agencies working in the PD diagnostics field.

records.title: Predictive value of multimodal models combining CT body composition and clinical variables for short-term postoperative complications in colorectal cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Predictive value of multimodal models combining CT body composition and clinical variables for short-term postoperative complications in colorectal cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Malnutrition and sarcopenic obesity are prevalent in colorectal cancer (CRC) and linked to adverse surgical outcomes. Conventional screening often overlooks this occult malnutrition. Preoperative computed tomography (CT)-based body composition analysis (BCA) provides objective biomarkers for muscle depletion and fat distribution. This systematic review evaluates multimodal machine learning (ML) models integrating BCA and clinical variables to predict CRC postoperative complications and inform precision nutrition strategies.

Methods

We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library (inception to April 13, 2026) for ML models predicting postoperative complications in CRC using BCA. Quality was assessed using PROBAST. Pooled area under the curve (AUC) was estimated via a random-effects model, alongside subgroup analyses.

Results

Eight studies (n = 7,835) were included. The pooled AUC was 0.84 (95% CI: 0.76-0.89), indicating good discriminative performance, although substantial heterogeneity was present (I 2 = 79.7%). Nomogram-based models showed a pooled AUC of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.78-0.92). For anastomotic leakage, the pooled AUC was 0.83 (95% CI: 0.35-0.98), although this estimate was imprecise because only two studies contributed to this subgroup.

Conclusion

Multimodal ML models integrating BCA biomarkers offer a robust, data-driven framework for preoperative risk stratification in CRC. Identifying high-risk body composition phenotypes may facilitate tailored prehabilitation and targeted immunonutrition strategies. Future efforts must prioritize standardized BCA and multi-center external validation.

Systematic review registration

CRD420261364363.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence for Predicting Treatment Response in Patients With Anxiety Disorders After Cognitive Behavioral Therapy: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence for Predicting Treatment Response in Patients With Anxiety Disorders After Cognitive Behavioral Therapy: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Artificial intelligence (AI) models have been increasingly explored for predicting treatment response to cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) in patients with anxiety disorders. Identifying potential responders in advance may help inform treatment planning and support clinical decision-making. Although a growing number of studies have applied AI techniques in this context, reported performance estimates vary across studies, and the overall predictive accuracy has not been comprehensively quantified.

Objective

This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to quantify the overall performance of AI models in predicting treatment response following CBT for anxiety disorders and to examine how data sources, algorithmic approaches, and diagnostic subtypes influence predictive performance.

Methods

A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and PsycINFO up to August 2025. We included studies that validated AI models for predicting CBT treatment response (remission or response) in patients diagnosed with an anxiety disorder. The risk of bias was assessed using the PROBAST+AI (Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool for Artificial Intelligence) tool. Predictive performance metrics, including sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and area under the curve (AUC), were extracted and pooled. Pooled estimates for sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic accuracy were derived using the Restricted Maximum Likelihood estimator, with CIs adjusted via the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman method. Prediction intervals were calculated and reported alongside these pooled estimates to illustrate the expected distribution of effects in real-world settings.

Results

Eleven studies were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled sensitivity of AI-based models for predicting treatment response was 0.73 (95% CI 0.58-0.85; I²=82.8%), and the pooled specificity was 0.75 (95% CI 0.59-0.89; I²=96.7%). The overall pooled accuracy was 0.74 (95% CI 0.62-0.84; I²=94.6%). The summary AUC was 0.81 (95% CI 0.78-0.85), indicating moderate discriminative performance. Subgroup analyses showed that models incorporating multimodal data achieved superior predictive performance, with a pooled sensitivity of 0.84 and an accuracy of 0.82. In addition, predictive performance was the highest in patients with social anxiety disorder compared with other anxiety disorder subtypes.

Conclusions

This meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized AI performance in predicting CBT response for anxiety disorders, moving beyond narrative reviews to provide pooled evidence. In contrast to existing reviews that encompass broader diagnostic groups, our focused approach establishes a precise benchmark for this clinical domain, highlighting the current moderate overall performance. Furthermore, we extend beyond previous work by demonstrating the superior predictive utility of multimodal data, identifying social anxiety disorder as the most predictable subtype, and systematically evaluating the impact of data modalities and algorithm types. Future efforts should prioritize robustly validated multimodal models, laying essential groundwork for the potential development of AI-assisted tools to personalize treatment planning in anxiety disorders.

records.title: Generative AI and student motivation: an SDT-guided systematic review of learning activities, motivational regulation, and measurement.

content.title: Generative AI and student motivation: an SDT-guided systematic review of learning activities, motivational regulation, and measurement.
content.abstract: The application of Generative AI is reshaping students' learning. However, student motivation in GenAI-supported learning is complex and influenced by multiple factors. To fully realize the educational potential of GenAI, a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between student motivation and GenAI is necessary. To address this gap, this study conducted a systematic literature review. From the perspective of Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this review examined 39 articles published between 2023 and 2025, drawn from two databases: Web of Science and Scopus. This study provides three major findings. First, competence-related learning activities were the most frequently identified across the reviewed studies. Second, four categories were reported in relation to student motivation: GenAI characteristics, learner factors, psychological factors, and environmental factors. Third, three major aspects of motivational conceptualization are basic psychological needs, motivation construct, and motivation-related construct. In addition, quantitative questionnaires were the dominant approach used to measure these constructs. Finally, the relationship among these three findings is illustrated. The findings provide insights into student motivation in GenAI-supported learning and highlight the relevance of GenAI characteristics, learners, and the learning environment. This study also provides theoretical and practical implications for facilitating students' motivation in GenAI-supported learning environments.

records.title: Performance of machine learning-based prediction models for hypoglycemia in Chinese patients with diabetes: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Performance of machine learning-based prediction models for hypoglycemia in Chinese patients with diabetes: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objectives

This study aimed to systematically evaluate the predictive performance of machine learning (ML)-based models for predicting hypoglycemia in Chinese patients with diabetes.

Methods

We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, CINAHL, CNKI, and Wanfang databases from inception to February 2026. Eligible studies focused on the development or validation of ML-based models for predicting hypoglycemia in Chinese patients with diabetes. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers. Information on study characteristics, modeling approaches, predictors, validation methods, and model performance was collected. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was synthesized using a random-effects model. Study quality was assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST).

Results

A total of 13 studies were included, and the pooled prevalence of hypoglycemia was 25% (95% CI: 17%-33%). The overall pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.90 (95% CI: 0.87-0.93). Subgroup analyses by modeling algorithms showed pooled AUCs of 0.89 for extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), 0.88 for random forest (RF), 0.85 for support vector machine (SVM), 0.84 for Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), 0.83 for logistic regression (LR), and 0.81 for decision tree (DT) models. Common predictors included age, insulin use, body mass index, HbA1c, creatinine, and history of hypoglycemia.

Conclusion

We attempted to provide a comprehensive overview of machine learning-based prediction models for hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes. Research in this field remains at an early stage, although several models with good discriminatory performance have been reported. Methodological limitations and insufficient validation were observed in many studies. Concerns regarding model robustness and interpretability also exist. More efforts to develop reliable and interpretable models and to promote their application in clinical practice for early risk identification are needed.

records.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence Models for Detecting Odontogenic Keratocytes on CBCT Imaging: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence Models for Detecting Odontogenic Keratocytes on CBCT Imaging: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Background and aims

Differentiating odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) from other radiolucent jaw lesions like ameloblastoma is clinically important but radiographically difficult. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) show promise for enhancing diagnosis using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). This study aims to systematically evaluate and meta-analyze the diagnostic accuracy of AI models in detecting OKCs on CBCT imaging.

Methods

A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to PRISMA-DTA guidelines. Five electronic databases were searched through July 6, 2025. Studies employing AI models for OKC detection using CBCT were included. Methodological quality was assessed using QUADAS-2. Pooled estimates were computed using a random-effects model, with heterogeneity evaluated via I2 and meta-regression. The Eager test and funnel plot were employed to assess publication bias.

Results

Twelve studies were included. AI models demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy, characterized by a pooled sensitivity of 89% (95% CI: 79%-95%) and specificity of 92% (95% CI: 81%-97%), both exceeding 85%, along with a substantial diagnostic odds ratio (87.06) and a robust discriminative ability (AUC = 0.828). Deep learning (DL) models achieved higher sensitivity (91%) than machine learning (ML) models (86%), while ML models showed slightly higher specificity. Heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 78%-93%). Publication year explained 57.2% of the variability in sensitivity.

Conclusions

AI-based models, particularly CNN-based DL architectures, demonstrate clinically relevant diagnostic performance with high sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic odds ratios, supporting their potential role as adjunctive tools in CBCT-based differentiation of OKCs from other odontogenic lesions.

records.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
content.abstract:
Background

Dietary protein supplements are commonly consumed to support increases in lean body mass among healthy adults engaged in resistance training (RT). Although whey protein has been extensively investigated, plant-based protein supplements have emerged as a viable alternative for individuals who avoid animal-derived products.

Methods

The present study aims to evaluate, through a systematic review and meta-analysis, the effects of plant-based versus whey protein supplementation on body composition in untrained adults (18-59 years) undergoing RT, using Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DEXA). The systematic review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 checklist and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251145410). Searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, identifying 5 studies that met the inclusion criteria for qualitative synthesis and meta-analysis.

Results

When combined with RT, both plant-based and whey protein supplementation were associated with improvements in lean body mass (LBM) and body fat mass (BFM), with no significant between-group differences observed.

Conclusions

Thus, soy- and pea-based protein supplements may support favorable body composition changes in adults initiating RT and could be considered practical nutritional options for individuals seeking alternatives to whey protein. Regarding chia-based protein, the available evidence is currently limited to a single study that did not demonstrate significant changes in lean body mass; therefore, firm conclusions regarding its efficacy cannot be drawn at this time.

records.title: Lower-Body Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Response to Concurrent Training in Trained Young Males.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Lower-Body Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Response to Concurrent Training in Trained Young Males.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Gomes, M, Costa, M, Pezarat-Correia, P, and Mendonca, GV. Lower-body strength and hypertrophy adaptations in response to concurrent training in trained young males. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study examined the interference effect of concurrent training (CT) on maximal and explosive strength and muscle morphology in trained young males. Thirty subjects were randomly assigned to endurance training (E), resistance training (R), or CT for 11 weeks. The intervention comprised 2 mesocycles: weeks 1-5 emphasizing maximal strength, and weeks 6-11 targeting explosive strength. Assessments were conducted at baseline, mid-training, and post-training, and included leg-press maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC), rate of force development (RFD), countermovement jump kinetics, and vastus lateralis cross-sectional area and pennation angle. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction increased only in the R group (18.4 ± 10.2%, p = 0.015). Peak RFD improved in both R (31.8 ± 23.2%) and CT (23.1 ± 27.9%), although with distinct time courses: R improved progressively across both mesocycles, whereas CT improved only during the second. Early-phase RFD (0-50 ms) increased in the R group from mid-training onward, whereas the CT group improved only from mid- to post-training (38.3 ± 40.4%, p = 0.021), accompanied by greater quadriceps electromyographic activity (p < 0.05). No changes in RFD were observed in E during training. Countermovement jump positive impulse improved in both R (12.7 ± 9.0%) and CT (8.8 ± 8.3%, p < 0.05), with no evidence of interference in jump-related explosive performance. Cross-sectional area increased in both R (17.0 ± 13.0%) and CT (8.8 ± 9.4%, p < 0.05). Pennation angle increased in CT (10.1 ± 12.9%) and R (18.6 ± 15.1%). These findings indicate that, although CT may limit MVIC development and delay early-phase RFD adaptations, it does not hinder explosive performance when resistance training is oriented toward rapid-strength development. Thus, CT can be effectively implemented in trained individuals when resistance training is periodized to emphasize neural-driven explosive or hypertrophy-related adaptations.

records.title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Chilingirian-Padrón, R, Álvarez-Yates, T, and García-García, O. Effects of in-season contrast strength training on jump performance and sprint ability in female field hockey players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 6-week in-season contrast strength training program incorporating sport-specific tasks on neuromuscular performance in sub-elite female field hockey players. Twenty-five athletes completed a pre-post single-cohort intervention integrated into their regular team schedule. Each session consisted of 3 sequential blocks: (a) a high-load strength exercise targeting maximal strength or hypertrophy (70-85% 1 repetition maximum [1RM]); (b) a biomechanically related explosive action performed at low load (∼30% 1RM) and high execution velocity; and (c) a high-speed sport-specific task. Jump performance was assessed using bilateral and unilateral countermovement jumps (CMJs) and free arm CMJ, whereas sprint ability was evaluated through 10- and 20-m sprints. A mixed-model repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to determine the effects of the intervention, with Time (Pre, Post) as within-subject factor and Playing Position (defenders, midfielders, forwards) as between-subject factor, with the level of significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements were observed in all jump and sprint assessments: jump performance increased by 5.7-29.6%, whereas sprint ability improved by 1.6-1.9%. These findings indicate that 6 weeks of contrast strength training incorporating high-speed sports-specific tasks performed during the competitive season elicited meaningful improvements in stretch-shortening cycle-related jump performance and sprint ability in sub-elite female field hockey players.

records.title: Comparison of Functional and Traditional Strength and Power Training on U19 Soccer Players During Offseason in Norway: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Comparison of Functional and Traditional Strength and Power Training on U19 Soccer Players During Offseason in Norway: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Engberg Treu Lassen, L, Kersting, UG, and Pessoto Hirata, R. Comparison of functional and traditional strength and power training on U19 soccer players during off-season in Norway: A randomized controlled trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Functional training emphasizes multiplanar, soccer-specific movement patterns requiring body control, whereas traditional resistance training focuses on maximal force production through stable, bilateral lifts. Although both approaches are common in soccer physical preparation, their relative effects on soccer-specific performance remain uncertain. This study compared the effects of functional vs. traditional strength training on performance outcomes during the offseason in U19 male players. Thirty-three Norwegian players were randomly allocated to a functional training group (FTG, n = 11), a traditional training group (TTG, n = 11), or a control group (CG, n = 11) using stratified, concealed allocation. During the first 4 weeks, all groups completed 2 weekly soccer sessions; FTG and TTG additionally completed 2 supervised 70-minute strength sessions per week. In the final 4 weeks, FTG and TTG continued the twice-weekly strength training, whereas CG ceased organized training. Functional training group performed unilateral, multiplanar free-weight exercises, while TTG performed bilateral, uniplanar machine-based exercises. The primary outcome was technical soccer performance, with mobility, dynamic balance, sprint speed, change of direction, and vertical jump as secondary outcomes. Both FTG and TTG improved Loughborough Soccer Shooting Test (LSST) performance compared with CG (FTG: -0.43 seconds, p = 0.003, d = 1.62; TTG: -0.50 seconds, p < 0.001, d = 1.88). Traditional training group also increased body mass compared with the CG (2.20 kg, p = 0.002, d = 1.65). Functional and traditional strength training produced comparable improvements in LSST time. These findings highlight training dose response and support individualized off-season programs integrating physical preparation with sport-specific demands.

records.title: Effects of Prolonged Combined Aerobic and Strength Training on Movement Velocities During a Strength Loading Bout: Targeting Same Versus Separate Muscle Groups.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effects of Prolonged Combined Aerobic and Strength Training on Movement Velocities During a Strength Loading Bout: Targeting Same Versus Separate Muscle Groups.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Feuerbacher, JF, Jacobs, MW, Dragutinovic, B, Rehbein, P, and Schumann, M. Effects of prolonged combined aerobic and strength training on movement velocities during a strength loading bout: targeting same versus separate muscle groups. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Combined aerobic and strength training may impair explosive strength performance, especially when targeting the same muscle groups. This study aimed to assess the effects of prolonged combined aerobic and strength training on movement velocities and velocity loss during a strength loading bout when the aerobic and strength training target the same vs. separate muscle groups. Thirty-two men participated in a 12-week intervention, divided into 3 groups: (a) LHLS (lower-body high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and strength training), (b) LHUS (lower-body HIIT and upper-body strength training), and (c) LSUS (lower- and upper-body strength training). Changes in the area under the mean propulsive velocity (MPV) and velocity-loss curves during strength loadings were analyzed pre- and postintervention. Squat performance was compared between LHLS and LSUS, while bench press performance was compared between LHUS and LSUS. The level of significance was set at ρ ≤ 0.05. During bench press loading, no statistically significant main effects for group ( p = 0.225), for timepoint ( p = 0.170), nor group × timepoint ( p = 0.943) were observed for MPV. In squat loading, a statistically significant main effect for timepoint was found ( p = 0.020), with a decrease in MPV for LHLS postintervention ( p = 0.006). The interaction between group and timepoint was not statistically significant ( p = 0.083). No statistically significant main effects for group ( p = 0.110, p = 0.076), for timepoint ( p = 0.590, p = 0.244), nor group × timepoint ( p = 0.626, p = 0.239) were observed for velocity loss in either bench press or squat loading. These findings suggest that explosive strength performance may be more susceptible to interference when aerobic and strength training target the same, rather than different, muscle groups.

records.title: The effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition and influence of FTO genotype in exercise-trained men and women.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: The effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition and influence of FTO genotype in exercise-trained men and women.
content.abstract:
Background

High-protein diets have consistently been associated with favorable changes in body composition in both sedentary and exercise-trained populations. Despite abundant evidence supporting protein intakes above the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for active individuals, the effects of deliberate protein overfeeding, particularly in those already consuming adequate protein, remain incompletely characterized. The primary purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition in exercise-trained men and women. The secondary purpose was to determine whether body composition adaptations differed by FTO rs9939609 genotype.

Methods

Fifty-six exercise-trained men and women (age: 22.40 ± 5.78 years; body mass: 75.47 ± 14.98 kg; BMI: 24.52 ± 3.50 kg/m2; resistance training: 5.12 ± 3.35 h/week) were enrolled in a 4-week dietary intervention. Participants were instructed to increase their daily protein intake by approximately 20% above baseline while maintaining habitual training. Body composition was assessed pre- and post-intervention using a multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance device (InBody® 270). Dietary intake was self-monitored via MyFitnessPal®. Thirty-five participants completed both pre- and post-testing assessments and constituted the primary analysis. Linear regression models adjusted for baseline values indicated that FTO genotype was not a significant predictor of body composition changes (p > 0.05).

Results

Protein intake trended toward a significant increase over the 4-week period (pre: 146 ± 66 g/day vs. post: 164 ± 79 g/day; p = 0.053), representing an approximate 12% increase. Total energy intake, carbohydrate, and fat intake did not significantly change. Lean body mass increased significantly (pre: 59.95 ± 14.14 kg vs. post: 60.62 ± 14.42 kg; p = 0.005; Cohen's d = 0.31) and total body water increased significantly (pre: 43.85 ± 10.35 L vs. post: 44.34 ± 10.55 L; p = 0.005). Fat mass (p = 0.424), body fat percentage (p = 0.149), and total body mass (p = 0.09) did not significantly change.

Conclusions

A 4-week modest protein overfeeding protocol in exercise-trained men and women was associated with a significant increase in lean body mass and total body water without concomitant increases in fat mass. These adaptations were not modified by FTO rs9939609 genotype. These findings support the contention that higher protein intakes do not promote fat accretion and may facilitate improvements in body composition in trained individuals.

records.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Sebastian-Rico, JM, Muñoz-Fernández, MJ, Martínez-Aranda, LM, Calvo-Lluch, Á, and Ortega-Becerra, M. Effectiveness of pelvic floor muscle training in women soccer players and its relationship with quality of life and pelvic floor muscle strength: a randomized controlled pilot study. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study investigated the effects of a 6-week pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) program on muscle strength, function, and the prevalence of related dysfunctions in professional female soccer players using a randomized controlled pilot study design. Twenty nulliparous professional soccer players from the Spanish professional league (2024-2025 season) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n = 12) or a control group (n = 8). Assessments included anthropometric data, validated questionnaires (International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire-Short Form and Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), clinical interviews, and physical examination using the PERFECT method and manometry. The intervention consisted of a 6-week supervised PFMT program (4 sessions/week, 30 minutes each) progressed through 4 phases: education, proprioception, strengthening, and functional integration. Results showed significant group × time interactions for pelvic floor self-efficacy (Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), with scores in the PFMT group increasing by 48.8 and 59.6% (p < 0.05), representing large between-group effect sizes (d = 0.91-1.26). Pelvic floor muscle performance increased by 122.4% in the intervention group (d = 1.25), whereas no meaningful changes were observed in the control group. No adverse events were reported. In conclusion, a 6-week supervised PFMT program is an effective and safe intervention for professional female soccer players, significantly improving muscle function and self-efficacy. These findings support the integration of PFMT for both therapeutic and preventive purposes in elite, high-impact sports environments.

records.title: Exploratory serum renal biomarker and eGFR responses to high-protein diets during resistance versus concurrent training in resistance-trained men.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Exploratory serum renal biomarker and eGFR responses to high-protein diets during resistance versus concurrent training in resistance-trained men.
content.abstract:
Background

High protein intake is common among resistance-trained athletes, but its association with renal biomarkers across different exercise modalities remains uncertain. This study investigated whether consuming a high-protein diet (3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹) during 16 weeks of resistance training (RT) or concurrent training (CT) affects renal biomarkers and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in resistance-trained men.

Methods

Forty-eight resistance-trained men (26 ± 6 years; BMI 25.6 ± 2.9 kg·m⁻²) were randomized to 16 weeks of RT or CT (4 sessions·wk⁻¹) while consuming either 1.6 or 3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ of protein in a 2 × 2 factorial design. Forty-four participants with complete pre- and post-intervention data were analyzed. Fasting blood samples were assessed for blood urea nitrogen (BUN), BUN/creatinine ratio, cystatin C, and eGFR calculated using the CKD-EPI creatinine (2021), cystatin C (2012), and creatinine-cystatin C (2021) equations. Within-group changes were evaluated using paired t-tests, and factorial effects were assessed using linear mixed-effects models (Time × Training × Protein).

Results

No statistically significant Time × Protein or Time × Training × Protein interactions were detected for any renal biomarker or eGFR estimate (all p ≥ 0.182). No significant within-group changes occurred in the 1.6 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ groups (all p > 0.05). In both 3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ groups, BUN and cystatin C increased (all p ≤ 0.017), while eGFR estimates decreased (all p ≤ 0.009). The BUN/creatinine ratio remained unchanged (p ≥ 0.614). However, these within-group findings were descriptive because the corresponding interaction effects were not statistically significant.

Conclusions

In resistance-trained men, 16 weeks of high protein intake did not produce statistically detectable differences in renal biomarker or eGFR changes compared with moderate protein intake, irrespective of training modality. Although modest increases in BUN and cystatin C and small decreases in eGFR estimates were observed within the high-protein groups, these findings were not supported by significant factorial interactions. The limited sample size precludes excluding clinically meaningful differences, warranting further investigation in larger studies.

records.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

records.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
content.abstract:
Purpose

The present study aimed to evaluate associations between resistance training and binge drinking in relation to musculoskeletal composition, physical fitness, cognitive function, and psychological wellness in young adult females.

Methods

Participants were categorized into four groups: sedentary low alcohol consumers (SL; n=12), sedentary binge drinkers (SB; n=12), resistance-trained low alcohol consumers (RTL; n=12), and resistance-trained binge drinkers (RTB; n=12). Measurements included body composition via DEXA scan, muscle quality via ultrasonography, and insulin sensitivity via oral glucose tolerance test. Physical performance was assessed using maximum chair stand power, vertical jump, broad jump, knee extensor torque, grip strength, and push-ups to failure. Tests and questionnaires were used to assess cognitive function and psychological wellness.

Results

Resistance-trained females had lower body fat than sedentary females (RTL = 29.28±4.27%; RTB = 29.03±3.67%; SL = 37.18±5.32%; SB = 34.83±3.54%; p<0.05), and RTL had more fat-free mass than SL and SB (RTL = 48.31±5.81 kg; SL = 38.08±6.59 kg; SB = 40.37±6.05 kg; both p<0.05). There were no differences between RTL and RTB in bone mineral density, muscle quality, or physical performance. RTL outperformed SL and SB on vertical jump (both p<0.05) while RTB outperformed SL and SB on broad jump. RTL had lower fasting blood glucose than RTB (88.92±12.09 mg/dL and 103.17 ± 10.21 mg/dL, respectively; p=0.008), and lower postprandial blood glucose than all groups (RTL = 103.83±19.82 mg/dL; RTB = 137.58±21.54 mg/dL; SL = 148.50±44.60 mg/dL; SB = 139.25±14.49 mg/dL; all p<0.05).

Conclusions

The results suggest that ≥1 year of binge drinking is associated with poorer metabolic health without differences in performance in young females. Further, frequent RT may mitigate the effects of binge drinking on body composition.

records.title: Multiple Sessions of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Combined With Squat Training Improve Lower-Limb Maximum Strength in Healthy Adult Men.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Multiple Sessions of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Combined With Squat Training Improve Lower-Limb Maximum Strength in Healthy Adult Men.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Yan, X, Zuo, Z, Nitsche, MA, Zhang, X, and Qi, F. Multiple sessions of transcranial direct current stimulation combined with squat training improve lower-limb maximum strength in healthy adult men. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to investigate the effects of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with Squat training (ST) on lower-limb maximum strength in healthy adult men. Sixty men (age: 21.6 ± 2.1 years, height: 177.5 ± 5.3 cm, body mass: 73.1 ± 7.4 kg) were randomly assigned to 4 groups (tDCS + ST group, sham tDCS + ST group, tDCS + rest group, sham tDCS + rest group). The 6-week intervention program was implemented with biweekly sessions, totaling 12 treatment sessions, each separated by a minimum 48-hour interval. After the tDCS intervention, the ST groups performed squat exercises while the tDCS + rest and sham tDCS + rest groups sat quietly for 30 minutes. Lower-limb maximal muscle strength was measured at 4 distinct time points: preintervention (T0), 24 hours post-third week intervention (T1), 24 hours post-sixth week final session (T2), and 1 week post-entire intervention completion (T3). Key evaluation metrics were measured, including 1 repetition maximum (1RM) squat, knee extensor and flexor peak torque, and rectus femoris cross-sectional area (CSA). Significant improvements in 1RM, knee extensor strength, and nondominant rectus femoris CSA were observed in both tDCS + ST and sham tDCS + ST groups compared with the sham tDCS-only group (p < 0.05). No differences in knee strength, 1RM, or rectus femoris CSA were observed between the tDCS + rest and sham tDCS + rest groups. The results indicate that anodal tDCS combined with ST does not yield additional training benefits on lower-limb maximal strength in healthy adults when compared with ST alone.

records.title: Do Athletes Lose Soleus Strength Over the Course of a Season? Longitudinal Monitoring of Seated Plantar Flexion Maximum Voluntary Contraction Strength and Factors That Affect It in Australian Football Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Do Athletes Lose Soleus Strength Over the Course of a Season? Longitudinal Monitoring of Seated Plantar Flexion Maximum Voluntary Contraction Strength and Factors That Affect It in Australian Football Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Green, B, Pizzari, T, Schache, AG, Rio, EK, Evans, SCS, Cooper, S, and Murphy, MC. Do athletes lose soleus strength over the course of a season? Longitudinal monitoring of seated plantar flexion maximum voluntary contraction strength and factors that affect it in Australian football players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The calf muscles are critical to dynamic lower-limb function in sports but are susceptible to injury. Despite its role in performance and injury, research has not evaluated soleus strength changes over the course of a season, or factors affecting it. Flexed-knee maximum plantar flexion strength was longitudinally monitored in state-league Australian footballers (2 Western Australian and 1 Victorian team) across 1-season at timepoints: preseason (T0), early in-season (T1), late in-season (T2). Generalized estimating equations evaluated strength outcomes over time (absolute, relative, asymmetry). Intrinsic factors (e.g., age, sex, injury history, sport exposure history, calf-focused resistance training) were analyzed to determine longitudinal associations with strength. Forty-one athletes (32 male, 9 female) were monitored across 210 strength measurements from T0 to T2. Absolute (T0 = 121.7 ± 27 kg; T1 = 135.2 ± 27.3 kg; T2 = 135.8 ± 25.9 kg) and relative (T0 = 1.51 ± 0.28 body mass [BM]; T1 = 1.69 ± 0.27 BM, T2 = 1.75 ± 0.26 BM) strength demonstrated longitudinal change (absolute: β = 19.33 kg, relative: β = 0.24 BM; p < 0.001). Reduced strength was associated with a recent calf injury history (relative and absolute: p < 0.001) and older age (p = 0.03). Lower strength (absolute: β = -23.53 kg, relative: β = -0.22 BM; p < 0.05) and larger asymmetry (β = 8.13 kg, p = 0.01) were detected in female athletes. Athletes can be expected to improve and maintain soleus capacity across seasonal periods. Athlete age, calf injury history, and sex can affect strength longitudinally. These findings may guide individualized prevention, performance, and postinjury benchmarking.

records.title: An Automated Blood Flow Restriction Device Is Reliable, but Not Valid, for Determining Lower Limb Occlusion Pressure in Resistance-trained Adults.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: An Automated Blood Flow Restriction Device Is Reliable, but Not Valid, for Determining Lower Limb Occlusion Pressure in Resistance-trained Adults.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Lang, D, Fallo, X, and Bennett, H. An automated blood flow restriction device is reliable, but not valid, for determining lower limb occlusion pressure in resistance-trained adults. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Blood flow restriction (BFR) exercise can improve strength, hypertrophy, and aerobic performance. Accurate limb occlusion pressure (LOP) assessment is essential for safe prescription. The AirBands is a novel automated BFR device that estimates LOP using integrated sensors, making LOP assessment easier. However, its validity and reliability are not well established in resistance-trained individuals. This study evaluated the concurrent validity of the AirBands compared with a handheld Doppler ultrasound for lower limb LOP, and its test-retest reliability, in resistance-trained adults. Twenty-six resistance-trained adults (14 males, 12 females; 24.2 ± 4.7 years) participated. For validity, LOP was measured using AirBands and Doppler in randomized order, using the same cuff. For reliability, automated LOP was measured twice, 10 minutes apart. Agreement was assessed using Bland-Altman limits of agreement and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). No significant difference was observed between manual (231.7 ± 17.8 mm Hg) and automated (230.8 ± 38.3 mm Hg) LOP (mean difference -0.8 mm Hg; p = 0.928), although validity ICC was poor (0.236, 95% confidence interval [CI] = -0.293 to 0.641). Bland-Altman analysis indicated proportional bias, with overestimation at lower values and underestimation at higher values. Reliability showed no significant difference between test 1 (243.0 ± 37.5 mm Hg) and test 2 (242.3 ± 40.5 mm Hg) (mean difference 1.0 mm Hg; p = 0.816) and good reliability (ICC = 0.862, 95% CI = 0.715 to 0.936). AirBands demonstrates good test-retest reliability but poor concurrent validity vs. Doppler ultrasound. Clinicians should confirm automated values using a Doppler ultrasound before prescribing BFR.

records.title: Effects of extremely low-volume high-intensity interval training combined with iron supplementation versus iron supplementation alone on postural control in young women with iron deficiency anemia: a randomized controlled trial.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of extremely low-volume high-intensity interval training combined with iron supplementation versus iron supplementation alone on postural control in young women with iron deficiency anemia: a randomized controlled trial.
content.abstract:
Background

Recent research revealed postural control deterioration in young women with Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). To address this postural deficit, it is crucial to develop intervention strategies for postural rehabilitation in these individuals. This study aimed to explore the effect of 8-week extremely low-volume high-intensity interval training (HIIT) based on plyometric exercises combined with iron supplementation versus simple iron treatment on postural control of young women with IDA.

Methods

This randomized controlled trial enrolled young women with IDA aged 18-25 years, who were randomly assigned to a training group (TG; n = 16) or a non-training group (NTG; n = 17). All participants received oral iron supplementation (ferrous sulfate, 494.5 mg/day, administered as 247.25 mg twice daily), while the TG additionally completed an 8-week extremely low-volume HIIT program based on plyometric exercises. Hemoglobin (Hb) and serum ferritin concentrations were assessed, alongside muscle endurance, reaction time performance, and postural control. Muscle endurance was evaluated using the Killy test, reaction time performance using an online simple reaction time test, and postural control using a stabilometric platform under bipodal and semi-tandem stance conditions. Postural assessments were conducted with eyes open (EO) and eyes closed (EC) on firm and foam surfaces. All outcomes were measured at baseline and 72 h after the final intervention session.

Results

After the 8-week intervention, this study demonstrated significant improvements across both groups, irrespective of the intervention. However, TG showed significantly greater post-intervention improvements than NTG in Hb concentration (P = 0.042), muscle endurance (P < 0.001), and postural control. Superior postural control in TG was observed during a bipedal stance on a foam surface (EO: P = 0.001); EC: P = 0.035), as well as during semi-tandem stance on a firm surface (EO: P = 0.015; EC: P = 0.040) and on a foam surface (EO: P = 0.019; EC: P = 0.003), compared to the NTG. With a Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold for multiple comparisons (α = 0.00625), between-group differences in postural control remained significant for bipedal foam EO (P = 0.001) and semi-tandem foam EC (P = 0.003).

Conclusions

The study showed that women with IDA improved their postural performance regardless of the intervention used. However, an 8-week program of extremely low-volume HIIT combined with plyometric exercises and iron supplementation had a more beneficial effect compared to traditional iron therapy. These greater improvements in postural control occurred alongside greater improvements in the Hb concentration and muscle endurance in the TG compared to the NTG.

records.title: Self-Massage Acute Effects on Pressure Pain Threshold, Muscular Electrical Activity, and Muscle Force Production: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Self-Massage Acute Effects on Pressure Pain Threshold, Muscular Electrical Activity, and Muscle Force Production: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Furlan, MR, Machado, E, Petter, GdN, Barbosa, IM, Geremia, JM, and Glänzel, MH. Self-massage acute effects on pressure pain threshold, muscular electrical activity, and muscle force production: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 38(3): 620-635, 2024-Self-massage (SM) is often used in physiotherapy and sports training programs. However, the SM acute effects on pressure pain threshold (PPT), muscle electrical activity (MEA), and muscle force production remain unclear. A meta-analytical review was performed to verify the SM acute effects on neuromuscular responses in healthy adults or athletes. The review (CRD42021254656) was performed in the PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase databases. A synthesis of the included studies was performed, and both the risk of bias and the evidence certainty level were assessed through the PEDro scale and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach, respectively. Nineteen studies were included, 5 evaluated the PPT, 7 the thigh muscles' MEA, and 15 the lower-limb strength. The SM application induces moderate increases in quadriceps' PPT (5 studies; standardized mean difference [SMD]: 0.487; 95% CI 0.251-0.723; p < 0.001; I2 = 0%).
