We found no SM effects on the hamstrings and plantar flexors' MEA. Also, we observed small increases in knee extensors' concentric torque (2 studies; SMD: 0.288; 95% CI 0.088-0.489; p = 0.005; I2 = 0%), without effects in isometric muscle strength, eccentric torque, and rate of force development. Grading of recommendations assessment, development, and evaluation analysis showed high and low certainty levels for the SM effects on quadriceps' PPT and muscle strength, respectively. Self-massage pressure-volume application seems to be a determining factor in inducing changes in these parameters, and it may vary among the treated muscles, where a higher pressure-volume application is required for increasing knee flexors and plantar flexors' PPT and strength. Thus, new studies with better methodological quality should be performed to strengthen this evidence.

records.title: The Effects of High-Repetition Strength Training on Performance in Competitive Endurance Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: The Effects of High-Repetition Strength Training on Performance in Competitive Endurance Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Nugent, FJ, Flanagan, EP, Darragh, I, Daly, L, and Warrington, GD. The effects of high-repetition strength training on performance in competitive endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 37(6): 1315-1326, 2023-The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the effects of high-repetition strength training (HRST) on performance in competitive endurance athletes. The methodology followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis protocol. A search of databases was performed until December 2020. Inclusion criteria were (a) competitive endurance athletes, (b) ≥4 weeks HRST intervention, (c) control or comparison group, (d) outcome measures of performance (either physiological or time trial performance), and (e) all experimental designs. Quality assessment was performed using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro) scale. Of the 615 studies retrieved, 11 studies were included (216 subjects) and 9 studies provided sufficient data for the meta-analysis (137 subjects). The PEDro scale score had a mean of 5 of 10 points (range: 3-6). There was no significant difference between the HRST and control groups (g = 0.35; 95% confidence interval [CI] = -0.38 to 1.07; p = 0.35) or HRST and low-repetition strength training (LRST) groups (g = 0.24; 95% CI = -0.24 to 0.72; p = 0.33). The findings of this review and meta-analysis indicate that HRST does not result in improved performance over a 4- to 12-week period, and the results seem to be similar to LRST. The majority of studies involved recreational endurance athletes and had a mean duration of 8 weeks, which is a limitation of the findings. Future intervention studies should be > 12 weeks in duration and involve well-trained endurance athletes (maximal oxygen uptake [V̇o2max] of >65 ml·kg-1·min-2).

records.title: The effects of nicotine withdrawal on exercise-related physical ability and sports performance in nicotine addicts: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: The effects of nicotine withdrawal on exercise-related physical ability and sports performance in nicotine addicts: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Previous research has established that nicotine withdrawal can ameliorate cardiovascular and pulmonary function in smokers. Nevertheless, the impact on physical fitness and athletic performance remains under-investigated.

Objective

To evaluating the impacts of nicotine withdrawal on both exercise performance and exercise-associated physical capabilities in nicotine-dependent individuals.

Study design

A comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis.

Data sources

The data was compiled from databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Central, and EBSCO.

Study selection

The selection criteria required studies to elucidate the effects of nicotine withdrawal on exercise performance or exercise-related physical abilities. Moreover, the selected studies needed to provide discernible experimental results.

Data synthesis and analysis

The random effects model was employed in data analysis, utilizing the standardized mean difference (SMD) and the 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) to estimate participants' exercise performance and physical abilities, referencing the Mean ±SD during baseline and withdrawal states.

Results

Out of the selected studies, 10 trials were included, encompassing 13,538 participants aged 18 to 65 years. The findings suggest that nicotine withdrawal could potentially enhance sports performance (SMD = 0.45, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.88; I^2 = 83%), particularly in terms of aerobic capacity. Short-term nicotine withdrawal (spanning 12 to 24 hours) might lead to a decline in participants' physical abilities in certain aspects like reaction time and sustained attention (SMD = -0.83, 95% CI: -1.91 to 0.25; I^2 = 79%), whereas long-term withdrawal (lasting 48 hours or more) demonstrated an opposing trend (SMD = 0.25, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.39; I^2 = 81%). Overall, the results show that long-term nicotine withdrawal exhibited some positive impacts on sports performance and exercise-related physical ability, with the withdrawal duration being an indicator of subsequent physical performance.

Conclusions

Mid- to long-term (≥3 months) nicotine withdrawal significantly improved the exercisers' exercise-related physical ability and sports performance. Conversely, short-term (≤24 hours) nicotine withdrawal considerably hampered exercisers' performance and physical cognition. It is suggested that exercises avoid abrupt nicotine cessation prior to competitions, as long-term nicotine withdrawal has been shown to significantly enhance exercise-related physiological capacities and athletic performance. By referring to existing literatures we also found that athletes with existing nicotine addiction may could consume nicotine 15-30 minutes before competition to enhance athletic performance and physical function.PROSPERO registration number CRD42023411381.

records.title: Physiological and health demands of Formula 1 motor racing: a comprehensive review with driver performance coach insight.

content.title: Physiological and health demands of Formula 1 motor racing: a comprehensive review with driver performance coach insight.
content.abstract: There is a need to better understand the specific demands and characteristics of Formula 1 (eg, high accelerations/decelerations, environmental stress) to optimise driver performance and health; however, data are scarce and much of the knowledge is held within the sport by the teams, drivers and the drivers' Performance Coaches. This review combined all relevant published research data available for motor car drivers (considering what is known regarding the neuromuscular and strength characteristics (6 articles), and the metabolic, cardiovascular and thermoregulatory responses (19 articles)) with novel data collected using structured interviews with three elite Formula 1 Performance Coaches. The limited data suggest that Formula 1 drivers are not especially exceptional when it comes to aerobic fitness, stature or body mass, but there are some sport-specific adaptations, most notably augmented neck strength. Short-term and long-term interventions are routinely undertaken to minimise the risks associated with the g-forces (eg, neck strength straining) and thermal stress (eg, heat acclimation, precooling and per-cooling) experienced, but much of these strategies are based on experience and anecdotal evidence rather than data. The Performance Coaches highlighted discrepancies between the published data and their applied practice and provided insight on several aspects related to driver health and performance, including the greatest stressors and how drivers prepare for g-forces, heat, jetlag, travel and nutritional constraints. The Performance Coaches also identified key areas that should be further addressed in future studies related to maintaining driver health (eg, the unknown impact of porpoising on lower back injury risk).

records.title: Does Stretching Training Influence Muscular Strength? A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Does Stretching Training Influence Muscular Strength? A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Thomas, E, Ficarra, S, Nunes, JP, Paoli, A, Bellafiore, M, Palma, A, and Bianco, A. Does stretching training influence muscular strength? A systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression. J Strength Cond Res 37(5): 1145-1156, 2023-The aim of this study was to review articles that performed stretching training and evaluated the effects on muscular strength. Literature search was performed using 3 databases. Studies were included if they compared the effects on strength following stretching training vs. a nontraining control group or stretching training combined with resistance training (RT) vs. an RT-only group, after at least 4 weeks of intervention. The meta-analyses were performed using a random-effect model with Hedges' g effect size (ES). A total of 35 studies ( n = 1,179 subjects) were included in this review. The interventions lasted for a mean period of 8 weeks (range, 4-24 weeks), 3-4 days per week, applying approximately 4 sets of stretching of approximately 1-minute duration. The meta-analysis for the stretching vs. nontraining control group showed a significant small effect on improving dynamic (k = 14; ES = 0.33; p = 0.007) but not isometric strength (k = 8; ES = 0.10; p = 0.377), following static stretching programs (k = 17; ES = 0.28; p = 0.006). When stretching was added to RT interventions, the main analysis indicated no significant effect (k = 17; ES = -0.15; p = 0.136); however, moderator analysis indicated that performing stretching before RT sessions has a small but negative effect (k = 7; ES = -0.43; p = 0.014); the meta-regression revealed a significant negative association with study length (β = -0.100; p = 0.004). Chronic static stretching programs increase dynamic muscular strength to a small magnitude. Performing stretching before RT and for a prolonged time (>8 weeks) can blunt the strength gains to a small-to-moderate magnitude. Performing stretching in sessions distant from RT sessions might be a strategy to not hinder strength development.

records.title: Which ROMs Lead to Rome? A Systematic Review of the Effects of Range of Motion on Muscle Hypertrophy.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Which ROMs Lead to Rome? A Systematic Review of the Effects of Range of Motion on Muscle Hypertrophy.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Kassiano, W, Costa, B, Nunes, JP, Ribeiro, AS, Schoenfeld, BJ, and Cyrino, ES. Which ROMs lead to Rome? a systematic review of the effects of range of motion on muscle hypertrophy. J Strength Cond Res 37(5): 1135-1144, 2022-Resistance exercise range of motion (ROM) influences muscular adaptations. However, there are no consistent practical guidelines about the optimal ROM for maximizing muscle hypertrophy. The objective of this article was to systematically review the literature for studies that compared the effects of full ROM (fROM) and partial ROM (pROM) on muscle hypertrophy. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science databases were searched to identify articles from the earliest record up to and including April 2022. We calculated the effect size (ES) scores of the variables of interest. Eleven studies were included in the review. Full ROM and pROM performed in the initial part of the ROM elicited greater muscle hypertrophy of the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, biceps brachii, and brachialis distal sites (between-groups ES: 0.20-0.90) than pROM performed in the final part of the ROM. fROM elicited greater muscle growth on the gluteus maximus and adductors than pROM in the final part of the ROM (between-groups ES: 0.24-0.25). Initial pROM produced more favorable proximal rectus femoris hypertrophy than fROM (between-groups ES: 0.35-0.38). pROM in the middle part of the ROM elicited greater triceps brachii hypertrophy than fROM (between-group ES: 1.21). In conclusion, evidence suggests that when training at a longer muscle length-through either pROM or fROM-some muscles, such as quadriceps femoris, biceps brachii, and triceps brachii, tend to experience optimal growth. Thus, the use pROM in the initial part of the excursion in combination with fROM training should be considered when prescribing hypertrophy-oriented resistance training programs.

records.title: Effects of Physical Training and Associations Between Physical Performance Characteristics and Golf Performance in Female Players: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effects of Physical Training and Associations Between Physical Performance Characteristics and Golf Performance in Female Players: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Robinson, L, Murray, A, Ehlert, A, Wells, J, Jarvis, P, Turner, A, Glover, D, Coughlan, D, Hembrough, R, and Bishop, C. Effects of physical training and associations between physical performance characteristics and golf performance in female players: A systematic review with meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 37(12): e646-e655, 2023-The aims of this systematic review were to assess the association between physical performance and measures of golf performance, and the effects of physical training on measures of golf performance, in female golfers. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Medline, and CINAHL. Inclusion criteria required studies to (a) have conducted a physical training intervention of any duration in female players and determine the effects on measures of golf performance, (b) determine the association between physical performance in at least one test and golf performance in female players, and (c) be peer-reviewed and published in English language. Methodological quality was assessed using a modified version of the Downs and Black Quality Index tool, and heterogeneity was examined through the Q statistic and I2 . Pooled effect sizes were calculated using standardized mean differences (SMDs) (with 95% confidence interval [CI]s) within a random-effects model, with Egger's regression test used to assess small study bias (inclusive of publication bias). Of the 2,378 articles screened, only 9 were included in the final review, with 3 of these being associative by design and 6 being training interventions. From an associative standpoint, clubhead speed (CHS) was reported in all 3 studies and was associated with measures of strength ( r = 0.54), lower-body power ( r = 0.60), upper-body power ( r = 0.56-0.57), and flexibility ( r = 0.52-0.71). When assessing the effects of physical training interventions, CHS was again the most commonly reported golf outcome measure ( n = 5). The random-effect model indicated that CHS significantly improves within each training group following training interventions (SMD = 0.73 [95% CIs: 0.32-1.14], Z = 3.50, p < 0.001), with trivial heterogeneity ( I2 = 0.00%, Q = 0.18; p = 0.9963) and no prevalence of small study bias depicted through the Egger's regression test ( z = -0.28, p = 0.78). From the available research, it seems that CHS can be positively affected from strength, power, and flexibility training interventions. From an associative standpoint, only 3 studies have been conducted solely in female players, with one showcasing questionable methodology. Future research should aim to carefully select test measures which better represent the physical capacities needed for the sport when determining the effects of and relationships with golf performance.

records.title: Exercise as medicine for depressive symptoms? A systematic review and meta-analysis with meta-regression.

content.title: Exercise as medicine for depressive symptoms? A systematic review and meta-analysis with meta-regression.
content.abstract:
Objective

To estimate the efficacy of exercise on depressive symptoms compared with non-active control groups and to determine the moderating effects of exercise on depression and the presence of publication bias.

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis with meta-regression.

Data sources

The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, SPORTDiscus, PsycINFO, Scopus and Web of Science were searched without language restrictions from inception to 13 September2022 (PROSPERO registration no CRD42020210651).

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Randomised controlled trials including participants aged 18 years or older with a diagnosis of major depressive disorder or those with depressive symptoms determined by validated screening measures scoring above the threshold value, investigating the effects of an exercise intervention (aerobic and/or resistance exercise) compared with a non-exercising control group.

Results

Forty-one studies, comprising 2264 participants post intervention were included in the meta-analysis demonstrating large effects (standardised mean difference (SMD)=-0.946, 95% CI -1.18 to -0.71) favouring exercise interventions which corresponds to the number needed to treat (NNT)=2 (95% CI 1.68 to 2.59). Large effects were found in studies with individuals with major depressive disorder (SMD=-0.998, 95% CI -1.39 to -0.61, k=20), supervised exercise interventions (SMD=-1.026, 95% CI -1.28 to -0.77, k=40) and moderate effects when analyses were restricted to low risk of bias studies (SMD=-0.666, 95% CI -0.99 to -0.34, k=12, NNT=2.8 (95% CI 1.94 to 5.22)).

Conclusion

Exercise is efficacious in treating depression and depressive symptoms and should be offered as an evidence-based treatment option focusing on supervised and group exercise with moderate intensity and aerobic exercise regimes. The small sample sizes of many trials and high heterogeneity in methods should be considered when interpreting the results.

records.title: Aspetar clinical practice guideline on rehabilitation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

content.title: Aspetar clinical practice guideline on rehabilitation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
content.abstract: This guideline was developed to inform clinical practice on rehabilitation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and was performed in accordance with the Appraisal of Guidelines for REsearch & Evaluation II (AGREE II) instrument and used the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. A Guideline Development Group systematically searched and reviewed evidence using randomised clinical trials and systematic reviews to evaluate the effectiveness of rehabilitation interventions and guide clinicians and patients on the content of the optimal rehabilitation protocol after ACLR.The guideline targets patients during rehabilitation after ACLR and investigates the effectiveness of the available interventions to the physiotherapist, alone or in combination (eg, exercise, modalities, objective progression criteria). Exercise interventions should be considered the mainstay of ACLR rehabilitation. However, there is little evidence on the dose-response relationship between volume and/or intensity of exercise and outcomes. Physical therapy modalities can be helpful as an adjunct in the early phase of rehabilitation when pain, swelling and limitations in range of motion are present. Adding modalities in the early phase may allow earlier pain-free commencement of exercise rehabilitation. Return to running and return to training/activity are key milestones for rehabilitation after ACLR. However, there is no evidence on which progression or discharge criteria should be used.While there is a very low level of certainty for most components of rehabilitation, most of the recommendations provided in this guideline were agreed to by expert clinicians. This guideline also highlights several new elements of ACLR management not reported previously.

records.title: Narrative Review of Sex Differences in Muscle Strength, Endurance, Activation, Size, Fiber Type, and Strength Training Participation Rates, Preferences, Motivations, Injuries, and Neuromuscular Adaptations.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Narrative Review of Sex Differences in Muscle Strength, Endurance, Activation, Size, Fiber Type, and Strength Training Participation Rates, Preferences, Motivations, Injuries, and Neuromuscular Adaptations.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Nuzzo, JL. Narrative review of sex differences in muscle strength, endurance, activation, size, fiber type, and strength training participation rates, preferences, motivations, injuries, and neuromuscular adaptations. J Strength Cond Res 37(2): 494-536, 2023-Biological sex and its relation with exercise participation and sports performance continue to be discussed. Here, the purpose was to inform such discussions by summarizing the literature on sex differences in numerous strength training-related variables and outcomes-muscle strength and endurance, muscle mass and size, muscle fiber type, muscle twitch forces, and voluntary activation; strength training participation rates, motivations, preferences, and practices; and injuries and changes in muscle size and strength with strength training. Male subjects become notably stronger than female subjects around age 15 years. In adults, sex differences in strength are more pronounced in upper-body than lower-body muscles and in concentric than eccentric contractions. Greater male than female strength is not because of higher voluntary activation but to greater muscle mass and type II fiber areas. Men participate in strength training more frequently than women. Men are motivated more by challenge, competition, social recognition, and a desire to increase muscle size and strength. Men also have greater preference for competitive, high-intensity, and upper-body exercise. Women are motivated more by improved attractiveness, muscle "toning," and body mass management. Women have greater preference for supervised and lower-body exercise. Intrasexual competition, mate selection, and the drive for muscularity are likely fundamental causes of exercise behaviors in men and women. Men and women increase muscle size and strength after weeks of strength training, but women experience greater relative strength improvements depending on age and muscle group. Men exhibit higher strength training injury rates. No sex difference exists in strength loss and muscle soreness after muscle-damaging exercise.

records.title: The Repeated Bout Effect of Multiarticular Exercises on Muscle Damage Markers and Physical Performances: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: The Repeated Bout Effect of Multiarticular Exercises on Muscle Damage Markers and Physical Performances: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Doma, K, Matoso, B, Protzen, G, Singh, U, and Boullosa, D. The repeated bout effect of multiarticular exercises on muscle damage markers and physical performances: a systematic review and meta-analyses. J Strength Cond Res 37(12): 2504-2515, 2023-This systematic review and meta-analysis compared muscle damage markers and physical performance measures between 2 bouts of multiarticular exercises and determined whether intensity and volume of muscle-damaging exercises affected the outcomes. The eligibility criteria consisted of (a) healthy male and female adults; (b) multiarticular exercises to cause muscle damage across 2 bouts; (c) outcome measures were compared at 24-48 hours after the first and second bouts of muscle-damaging exercise; (d) at least one of the following outcome measures: creatine kinase (CK), delayed onset of muscle soreness (DOMS), muscle strength, and running economy. Study appraisal was conducted using the Kmet tool, whereas forest plots were derived to calculate standardized mean differences (SMDs) and statistical significance and alpha set a 0.05. After screening, 20 studies were included. The levels of DOMS and CK were significantly greater during the first bout when compared with the second bout at T24 and T48 (p < 0.001; SMD = 0.51-1.23). Muscular strength and vertical jump performance were significantly lower during the first bout compared with the second bout at T24 and T48 (p ≤ 0.05; SMD = -0.27 to -0.40), whereas oxygen consumption and rating of perceived exertion were significantly greater during the first bout at T24 and T48 (p < 0.05; SMD = 0.28-0.65) during running economy protocols. The meta-analyses were unaffected by changes in intensity and volume of muscle-damaging exercises between bouts. Multiarticular exercises exhibited a repeated bout effect, suggesting that a single bout of commonly performed exercises involving eccentric contractions may provide protection against exercise-induced muscle damage for subsequent bouts.

records.title: Muscle-strengthening activities are associated with lower risk and mortality in major non-communicable diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies.

content.title: Muscle-strengthening activities are associated with lower risk and mortality in major non-communicable diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies.
content.abstract:
Objective

To quantify the associations between muscle-strengthening activities and the risk of non-communicable diseases and mortality in adults independent of aerobic activities.

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies.

Data sources

MEDLINE and Embase were searched from inception to June 2021 and the reference lists of all related articles were reviewed.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Prospective cohort studies that examined the association between muscle-strengthening activities and health outcomes in adults aged ≥18 years without severe health conditions.

Results

Sixteen studies met the eligibility criteria. Muscle-strengthening activities were associated with a 10-17% lower risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease (CVD), total cancer, diabetes and lung cancer. No association was found between muscle-strengthening activities and the risk of some site-specific cancers (colon, kidney, bladder and pancreatic cancers). J-shaped associations with the maximum risk reduction (approximately 10-20%) at approximately 30-60 min/week of muscle-strengthening activities were found for all-cause mortality, CVD and total cancer, whereas an L-shaped association showing a large risk reduction at up to 60 min/week of muscle-strengthening activities was observed for diabetes. Combined muscle-strengthening and aerobic activities (versus none) were associated with a lower risk of all-cause, CVD and total cancer mortality.

Conclusion

Muscle-strengthening activities were inversely associated with the risk of all-cause mortality and major non-communicable diseases including CVD, total cancer, diabetes and lung cancer; however, the influence of a higher volume of muscle-strengthening activities on all-cause mortality, CVD and total cancer is unclear when considering the observed J-shaped associations.

Systematic review registration

PROSPERO CRD42020219808.

records.title: Identifying evidence-practice gaps for shoulder injury risk factors in competitive swimmers: uniting literature and expert opinion.

content.title: Identifying evidence-practice gaps for shoulder injury risk factors in competitive swimmers: uniting literature and expert opinion.
content.abstract:
Objectives

To identify evidence-practice gaps regarding shoulder injury risk factors in competitive swimmers.

Methods

We gathered insights from 27 swimming experts including elite swimmers, coaches, high-performance staff and applied researchers using Concept Mapping. Participants brainstormed, sorted and rated (from 1 (least) to 10 (most) important and modifiable) their ideas of shoulder injury risk factors in competitive swimmers. Proposed risk factors rated above the grand mean for importance (6.2±0.4) or modifiability (6.5±0.5) ratings were considered highly important/modifiable. Expert opinions were then juxtaposed with systematic review findings to identify overlaps or convergences.

Results

Brainstorming generated 126 proposed shoulder injury risk factors for competitive swimmers, subsequently refined to 61 unique proposed risk factors by removing duplicates and combining similar responses. The participants sorted the 61 risk factors into seven distinct clusters. Experts perceived 36/61 proposed risk factors as highly important, of which 6 were supported by literature, 6 showed no association with injury, 2 had conflicting evidence and the remaining 22 have not yet been investigated, suggesting an evidence-practice gap. Three proposed risk factors 'inconsistent training load', 'poor stroke technique' and 'low posterior shoulder strength-endurance' exhibited high perceived importance, high perceived modifiability and supporting evidence.

Conclusion

An evidence-practice gap was identified for 28 proposed risk factors perceived as highly important by swimming experts despite either (1) no relevant empirical research (n=22), or (2) no association with injury (n=6) from synthesised evidence. Greater collaboration between researchers and practitioners is needed to effectively address shoulder injury risk factors in competitive swimmers.

records.title: Why does it work? Proposed biomedical effect mechanisms of exercise-based injury prevention programmes in football (soccer) and handball: a scoping review of 104 studies.

content.title: Why does it work? Proposed biomedical effect mechanisms of exercise-based injury prevention programmes in football (soccer) and handball: a scoping review of 104 studies.
content.abstract:
Objective

To describe the proposed biomedical effect mechanisms in research on exercise-based injury prevention programmes in football (soccer) and handball.

Design

Scoping review of randomised controlled trials (RCT), cohort studies and case studies.

Data sources

MEDLINE via PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science databases were searched from 2000 to 2024.

Eligibility criteria

Studies were included if they described exercise-based injury prevention programmes in football (soccer) or handball and provided a biomedical rationale or proposition of effect mechanisms. Peer-reviewed studies of all ages and both sexes at elite, subelite or amateur level were eligible.

Results

We included 104 studies (78 RCTs, 25 cohort studies, 1 case study) with sample sizes ranging from 10 to 4556 participants. Most studies (83%) were published after 2010, and interventions were reported to have an effect in 82% of the studies. Four main themes emerged describing the proposed effect mechanisms: neuromuscular control (47%), strength (39%), range of motion (11%) and physical fitness (3%). Definitions of key terms related to the intervention were provided in only 19% of studies, measurements of specific biomedical effect mechanisms were conducted in just 59% of studies.

Conclusion

Neuromuscular control and strength were the predominant proposed effect mechanisms for injury prevention programmes in football and handball. To better establish effect mechanisms of exercise-based interventions, future research should consistently define key terms related to the interventions and strive to identify and test causal mechanisms to optimise injury prevention programmes.

records.title: Does Varying Resistance Exercises Promote Superior Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains? A Systematic Review.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Does Varying Resistance Exercises Promote Superior Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains? A Systematic Review.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Kassiano, W, Nunes, JP, Costa, B, Ribeiro, AS, Schoenfeld, BJ, and Cyrino, ES. Does varying resistance exercises promote superior muscle hypertrophy and strength gains? A systematic review. J Strength Cond Res 36(6): 1753-1762, 2022-Fitness professionals routinely employ a variety of resistance training exercises in program design as a strategy to enhance muscular adaptations. However, it remains uncertain whether such an approach offers advantages over a fixed-exercise selection. The objective of this review was to review the effects of exercise variation on muscle hypertrophy and strength. A search of the literature was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science databases. Eight studies were identified as meeting inclusion criteria. The combined total sample of the studies was N = 241, comprising all young men. The methodological quality of included studies was considered "good" and "excellent" based on the Physiotherapy Evidence Database Scale. The available studies indicate that varying exercise selection can influence muscle hypertrophy and strength gains. Some degree of systematic variation seems to enhance regional hypertrophic adaptations and maximize dynamic strength, whereas excessive, random variation may compromise muscular gains. We conclude that exercise variation should be approached systematically with a focus on applied anatomical and biomechanical constructs; on the contrary, employing different exercises that provide a redundant stimulus, as well as excessive rotation of different exercises (i.e., high frequency of change), may actually hinder muscular adaptations.

records.title: Unilateral tests of lower-limb function as prognostic indicators of future knee-related outcomes following anterior cruciate ligament injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 150 adolescents and adults.

content.title: Unilateral tests of lower-limb function as prognostic indicators of future knee-related outcomes following anterior cruciate ligament injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 150 adolescents and adults.
content.abstract:
Objective

To investigate the prognostic capacity of individual hop tests, hop test batteries and other unilateral functional performance tests following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury.

Design

Systematic review with meta-analysis.

Data sources

Six databases searched up to June 2021.

Eligibility criteria

Studies reporting associations between unilateral lower-limb function (eg, hop tests) following ACL injury and future (≥3 months) knee-related outcomes.

Results

Of 42 included studies (13 150 participants), all assessed the single-forward hop test and 32 assessed a repeated-forward hop test (crossover hop, triple hop, 6m-timed hop), mostly within a year after ACL injury/reconstruction. Results of meta-analyses indicated that higher single-forward and repeated-forward hop limb symmetry were associated with higher odds of return-to-sport 1-3 years post-ACL reconstruction (OR 2.15; 95% CI 1.30 to 3.54; OR 2.11; 95% CI 1.23 to 3.60, respectively). Higher single-forward and repeated-forward hop limb symmetry was associated with better self-reported symptoms and function 1-37 years after ACL injury (OR 2.51; 95% CI 1.62 to 3.88; OR 4.28; 95% CI 1.65 to 11.08, respectively). Higher limb symmetry on a repeated-forward hop does not appear to be associated with higher odds of successful rehabilitation without ACL reconstruction (OR 1.51; 95% CI 0.94 to 2.44). Achieving ≥90% limb symmetry on the single-forward hop was associated with reduced odds of knee osteoarthritis 5-37 years after ACL injury (OR 0.46; 95% CI 0.23 to 0.94).

Conclusion

Very low certainty evidence suggests single-forward and repeated-forward hop tests are prognostic indicators for important knee-related outcomes in individuals after ACL injury and may help stratify individuals at risk of poor outcomes to target rehabilitation interventions.

Prospero registration number

CRD42018092197.

records.title: Common questions and misconceptions about protein supplementation: what does the scientific evidence really show?
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Common questions and misconceptions about protein supplementation: what does the scientific evidence really show?
content.abstract: Protein supplementation often refers to increasing the intake of this particular macronutrient through dietary supplements in the form of powders, ready-to-drink shakes, and bars. The primary purpose of protein supplementation is to augment dietary protein intake, aiding individuals in meeting their protein requirements, especially when it may be challenging to do so through regular food (i.e. chicken, beef, fish, pork, etc.) sources alone. A large body of evidence shows that protein has an important role in exercising and sedentary individuals. A PubMed search of "protein and exercise performance" reveals thousands of publications. Despite the considerable volume of evidence, it is somewhat surprising that several persistent questions and misconceptions about protein exist. The following are addressed: 1) Is protein harmful to your kidneys? 2) Does consuming "excess" protein increase fat mass? 3) Can dietary protein have a harmful effect on bone health? 4) Can vegans and vegetarians consume enough protein to support training adaptations? 5) Is cheese or peanut butter a good protein source? 6) Does consuming meat (i.e., animal protein) cause unfavorable health outcomes? 7) Do you need protein if you are not physically active? 8) Do you need to consume protein ≤ 1 hour following resistance training sessions to create an anabolic environment in skeletal muscle? 9) Do endurance athletes need additional protein? 10) Does one need protein supplements to meet the daily requirements of exercise-trained individuals? 11) Is there a limit to how much protein one can consume in a single meal? To address these questions, we have conducted a thorough scientific assessment of the literature concerning protein supplementation.

records.title: Echoes of the Modern Training Periodization Concepts in Russia Before the October 1917 Revolution.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Echoes of the Modern Training Periodization Concepts in Russia Before the October 1917 Revolution.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Bartolomei, S, Mammadova, G, Manno, R, Haff, GG, Hoffman, JR, and Merni, F. Echoes of the modern training periodization concepts in Russia before the October 1917 revolution. J Strength Cond Res 39(12): 1327-1330, 2025-The debate on the origins of the discipline of training periodization is still ongoing. The text "Olympic Sport," published by B. A. Kotov in 1916, was one of the first known books to focus on training methods and strategies for performance development. The book is also considered the first to deal with training organization and periodization. In addition, Kotov was the only author to cover these topics in Russia before the Soviet Bolshevik Revolution of October 1917. Recently, our research group had the opportunity to work on the original text published in 1916 in Russian, and on the article published with the pseudonym of "Boko" in 1913 for the journal "Russky Sport." The analysis of Kotov's articles offers an insight into periodization and training at the beginning of the 20th century. The knowledge of the historical events and of the evolution of sport allow this article to be contextualized and to understand the author's attempt to promote a different approach to athletic training. Relevant breakthroughs were included in this article, such as the use of training programs to organize long training periods, the prescription of submaximal training loads based on perceived effort and the use of specific preparation phases. In addition, the text contains one of the first notations of the concept of overtraining. Considering its novelty, "Olympic Sport" represents a revolutionary book and the author can be considered as a fundamental contributor to the development of the discipline of the training theory and a starting point of modern periodization.

records.title: Human Multi-Omics Meta-Analysis Identifies Molecular Layer-Specific Responses to Resistance and Endurance Exercise.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Human Multi-Omics Meta-Analysis Identifies Molecular Layer-Specific Responses to Resistance and Endurance Exercise.
content.abstract:
Purpose

Resistance and endurance exercise produce distinct adaptations, but molecular responses that distinguish these exercise modalities across studies and molecular layers remain incompletely defined. We sought to identify reproducible resistance- and endurance-associated molecular responses across human skeletal muscle and plasma omics datasets.

Methods

We integrated publicly available human exercise omics datasets. Random-effects meta-analyses included 15,312 genes from three skeletal muscle RNA-seq datasets and 4,641 proteins from two skeletal muscle proteomic datasets. Early skeletal muscle phosphoproteomic responses were compared across two independent studies using 2,430 matched phosphosites. At 24 hours, skeletal muscle phosphoproteomics and targeted and untargeted metabolomics in skeletal muscle and plasma were analyzed separately; plasma proteomics was not analyzed. Effects were standardized as resistance exercise minus endurance exercise, with significance defined within each molecular layer at FDR<0.05.

Results

RNA-seq identified 269 genes, including 71 resistance-associated and 198 endurance-associated genes. Global proteomics identified 10 proteins (nine resistance-associated; one endurance-associated). Early phosphoproteomic effects correlated across studies (r=0.589, P=4.1x10-227); 210 of 238 significant phosphosites were directionally concordant, and 51 met replication criteria. At 24 hours, targeted plasma metabolomics identified 14 endurance-associated features, while untargeted plasma metabolomics identified 18 features, including nine resistance-associated and nine endurance-associated features. Resistance-associated responses involved contractile, myofibrillar, cytoskeletal, extracellular matrix, protein quality-control, stress-response, and phosphorylation-related processes. Endurance-associated responses involved mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, respiratory-chain biology, fatty acid oxidation, substrate utilization, amino acid metabolism, and mitochondrial proteostasis.

Conclusions

Human molecular responses to resistance and endurance exercise are molecular-layer specific. Endurance-associated responses were more consistently represented in transcriptomic and metabolic layers, whereas resistance-associated responses were more prominent in protein abundance and phosphorylation. These findings provide a quantitative basis for selecting molecular measurements and sampling strategies in future human resistance and endurance exercise studies.

records.title: Large-Scale Evaluation of Performance and Biological Maturation in Post-PHV Youth Soccer Players: Sprinting, Jumping, Aerobic Fitness, and Functional Movement.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Large-Scale Evaluation of Performance and Biological Maturation in Post-PHV Youth Soccer Players: Sprinting, Jumping, Aerobic Fitness, and Functional Movement.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Akbaş, A, Hadyk, V, Bryk, P, Mazzei, S, Stanula, A, and Juras, G. Large-scale evaluation of performance and biological maturation in post-PHV youth soccer players: Sprinting, jumping, aerobic fitness, and functional movement. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to provide an integrated developmental profile of adolescent soccer players by examining how chronological age, biological maturation, and functional movement quality interact to shape sprint, jump, and aerobic fitness performance. A total of 246 male athletes (U15-U17) from 5 elite youth soccer academies completed sprint, jump, change-of-direction (COD), and aerobic tests alongside Functional Movement Screen (FMS) and Y-Balance Test (YBT) assessments. Maturity offset (years from peak height velocity, PHV) was used to estimate biological age, and group differences were analyzed using analysis of variance and analysis of covariance, with statistical significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements with age were observed in sprinting, jumping, and aerobic fitness (p < 0.001); however, after controlling for PHV, differences in jumping and COD performance were no longer significant, whereas sprint performance and aerobic fitness remained age-dependent. Functional movement and balance showed small age-related differences that were largely explained by maturational variation. Weak and inconsistent correlations between FMS, YBT, and performance (|r| ≈ 0.20-0.35) suggested partial independence between movement quality and motor output. Notably, in older players, higher scores in mobility-related FMS components were associated with slower sprinting, a pattern that may reflect-rather than cause-reduced mechanical efficiency associated with greater flexibility. These findings indicate that post-PHV players are not a homogeneous group and support the use of maturity-informed, multidimensional athlete monitoring to guide individualized training even after PHV.

records.title: Acute caffeine and carbohydrate strategies for fatigue-related sport-specific performance in team-sport athletes: a systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Acute caffeine and carbohydrate strategies for fatigue-related sport-specific performance in team-sport athletes: a systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Although caffeine and carbohydrate are established ergogenic strategies for physical performance, it remains unclear whether these benefits translate to the decision-making and sport-specific skills that determine team-sport performance under fatigue.

Methods

PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, and SPORTDiscus were searched on 28 July 2026. Thirty-one reports were retained; their reported analyzed sample sizes summed to 441 athletes. Twenty-three independent quantitative study clusters, with reported analyzed sample sizes summing to 341 athletes, contributed 67 effects. Multilevel random-effects models nested effect sizes within studies; primary assumptions were r = 0.5 and rho = 0.80. Inference used CR2 robust standard errors and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

Results

Soccer supplied 11 of the 23 quantitative clusters; every other sport category supplied four or fewer. Broad caffeine was centered near zero (Hedges' g = 0.040, 95% CI -0.211 to 0.291; p = 0.691; df = 4.41). Tier 1a perceptual-motor and Tier 1b technical/tactical estimates were imprecise. Broad carbohydrate was positive but uncertain (g = 0.256, 95% CI -0.094 to 0.605; p = 0.118; df = 4.96), and one study cluster materially influenced this estimate. All six GRADE comparisons were rated very low certainty. The two-study mental-fatigue calculation was too fragile for conventional inference.

Conclusions

Current evidence does not support assuming that the established physical ergogenic effects of caffeine translate to fatigue-related decision-making or sport-specific skill. Carbohydrate may provide a small benefit, but the evidence remains sparse and highly uncertain. Sensitivity to study composition was driven primarily by one influential cluster, whose omission increased the pooled estimate. The carbohydrate estimates apply only to heterogeneous ingested-beverage protocols and should not be extrapolated to mouth-rinse or gel strategies. Parallel syntheses do not establish intervention superiority or combined-strategy synergy.

records.title: The Respiratory Compensation Point Predicts 19.2-km Cycling Performance in Trained Male Cyclists.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: The Respiratory Compensation Point Predicts 19.2-km Cycling Performance in Trained Male Cyclists.
content.abstract:
Abstract

So, YLI, Faricier, R, Guluzade, NA, Belfry, GR, Murias, JM, and Keir, DA. The respiratory compensation point predicts 19.2-km cycling performance in trained male cyclists. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study tested the hypothesis that the step-ramp-step (SRS)-corrected cycling power output (PO) at the respiratory compensation point (RCP) predicts cycling time-trial performance and explored the independent and collective contributions to trial time of 4 physiological variables derived from single or repeated SRS protocols: peak oxygen uptake (V̇o2peak), cycling economy, RCP, and fatigue resistance. Twenty-eight trained male cyclists completed an SRS protocol before and after a 19.2-km virtual time trial (∼30 minutes) on their personal road bikes using a smart trainer. V̇o2peak, cycling economy, and SRS-corrected PO at RCP were derived from the pre-time-trial SRS protocol. Fatigue resistance was quantified as the change in peak ramp PO from pre- to post-time trial. Independent and multilinear regression evaluated the predictive strength of each variable. Relative SRS-corrected RCP (W·kg-1) showed the strongest independent correlation with time-trial completion time (r = -0.61, p < 0.001). Relative V̇o2peak (mL·kg-1·min-1) and cycling economy (%) were also moderately associated with time-trial performance (r = -0.42, p = 0.03; and r = -0.55, p < 0.001, respectively), whereas fatigue resistance was not significantly correlated. In the multilinear regression analysis, SRS-corrected RCP uniquely explained 30.9% of the model's total predictive variance (r = 0.68, p < 0.01) followed by cycling economy (21.3%), ΔPOpeak (2.1%), and absolute V̇o2peak (3.3%). Among trained male cyclists, relative PO at SRS-corrected RCP is a strong and independent predictor of ∼30-minute time-trial performance. The SRS protocol provides a practical, single-session method to assess key physiological determinants of endurance performance, with valuable applications for training prescription and athlete monitoring.

records.title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
content.abstract:
Background

Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes.

Methods

Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used.

Results

CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage.

Conclusions

Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.

records.title: Moderate-Intensity Interval Training Is Sufficient to Increase Muscle Mitochondrial Respiratory Capacity and Exercise Tolerance in Young Untrained Men.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Moderate-Intensity Interval Training Is Sufficient to Increase Muscle Mitochondrial Respiratory Capacity and Exercise Tolerance in Young Untrained Men.
content.abstract:
Introduction

There is considerable evidence that physical activity can stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis in muscles, enhance maximal mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate, improve physical fitness, and help maintain overall health in humans. On the other hand, there is growing evidence that excessive training load may have a detrimental effect on mitochondria and glucose homeostasis.

Hypothesis

We hypothesized that moderate-intensity interval training (MIIT) would be sufficient to increase muscle mitochondrial oxidative capacity and exercise tolerance in untrained healthy people.

Methods

Eleven young, healthy, untrained males took part in this study. They performed a 7-week endurance training program (MIIT) on a cycle ergometer, composed of 4 sessions per week, each lasting 40 min. Before and after the MIIT training program, a pulmonary maximal oxygen consumption (V̇O2max) as well as lactate threshold (LT) were determined and a muscle biopsy from the m. vastus lateralis was taken to evaluate the level of muscle proteins related to energy metabolism and mitochondrial biogenesis, and to measure the muscle's maximal mitochondrial respiration rate.

Results

The training resulted in an increase of skeletal muscle homogenate V̇O2max (by ~50%, P=0.001), due to increased mitochondrial mass and the enrichment of mitochondria with the individual respiratory chain complexes. The MIIT increased the power output at the lactate threshold (PO at LT) by ~43 W (P=0.001) and the pulmonary V̇O2max by 7% (P=0.01) and had no adverse effect on blood glucose homeostasis.

Conclusions

MIIT, which is a less intense form of training than the commonly used types of interval training, effectively induces a range of beneficial muscular and systemic adaptations that contribute to improvement of physical fitness and maintenances good health in humans.

records.title: Sex-specific Lower Limb Strength, Flexibility, and Running Biomechanics in Adolescents With and Without Osgood-Schlatter Disease.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Sex-specific Lower Limb Strength, Flexibility, and Running Biomechanics in Adolescents With and Without Osgood-Schlatter Disease.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To examine sex-specific lower limb strength, flexibility, and running biomechanics in adolescents with and without OSD.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective chart review of 100 adolescents (n=25 each group): females with OSD (age=14.6 ± 1.9 y; body mass index [BMI]=21.3 ± 2.1 kg/m2); males with OSD (age=14.4 ± 1.6 y; BMI=21.7 ± 3.2 kg/m2); females without OSD (age=14.8 ± 2.2 y; BMI=21.7 ± 3.0 kg/m2); and males without OSD (age=14.4 ± 2.2 y; BMI=22.0 ± 4.6 kg/m2). We assessed mass-normalized sagittal and frontal hip strength and sagittal knee strength via hand-held dynamometry, and quadriceps femoris (prone knee flexion) and hip flexor (Thomas test) flexibility. Limb crossover, contralateral pelvic drop [CPD], medial knee displacement, and tibial dominant stride were assessed during treadmill running. Group differences were analyzed using a two-way multivariate analysis of variance (continuous outcomes) and logistic regression (categorical outcomes), covarying for age and BMI. Analyses were performed using SPSS (alpha set at p<0.05).

Results

Compared with sex-matched healthy peers, females with OSD had impaired hip abduction strength and a greater propensity for CPD and medial knee displacement, though greater hip flexion strength (p≤0.03; Table). Males with OSD had greater hip and knee sagittal plane strength yet impaired flexibility (p≤0.02; Table). Compared with males with OSD, females with OSD had lower hip and knee strength, greater quadriceps femoris flexibility, and higher odds of frontal plane biomechanical deficits (p≤0.02; Table).

Conclusion

We observed sex-specific differences in lower limb muscular and biomechanical features in adolescents with OSD, suggesting that clinicians should consider sex-specific rehabilitation strategies for adolescents with OSD.

records.title: Should They Start or Not? A Comparative Analysis of Starter and Nonstarter Preseason Fitness Characteristics in NCAA Division III Baseball.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Should They Start or Not? A Comparative Analysis of Starter and Nonstarter Preseason Fitness Characteristics in NCAA Division III Baseball.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Schilling, DT, Abraham, TR, and Elazzazi, A. Should they start or not? A comparative analysis of starter and nonstarter preseason fitness characteristics in NCAA Division III baseball. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Preseason fitness testing in baseball is a widely adopted practice to assess the physical preparedness of players. However, the relationship between these preseason fitness assessments, their ability to differentiate starters from nonstarters in the subsequent season, and their relationship to preseason coaching evaluations is not well-established. This exploratory study aimed to provide a preseason profile of men's NCAA Division III baseball players, compare the differences between starting and nonstarting players, and explore the relationship of these preseason measures to the offensive performance of the starting players at the completion of the season. Starters were considered any hitter who averaged at least 2 plate appearances per team game played or participated in at least 75% of the team's games. Twenty-six players performed 8 preseason fitness tests; and the head coach, blinded to all preseason fitness testing results, subjectively rated the players' batting (power, ball contact, and form) and running performance (speed, agility, and form), resulting in a total offensive performance score (TOPS). In-season offensive performance was measured by each player's on-base plus slugging percentage (OPS). Starters demonstrated significantly greater batted ball velocity, countermovement vertical jump height, unilateral lateral to medial jump distance, medicine ball throw velocity, and faster 60-yard dash and agility T-test times relative to nonstarters. Notably, no significant correlations were observed between any physical performance variable and OPS or TOPS, suggesting that preseason fitness testing may reflect athletic readiness but does not directly relate to offensive performance or coaching evaluation outcomes in this sample.

records.title: Hematological and biochemical responses to three doses of caffeine during the CrossFit® workout: a randomized, double-blind, crossover trial.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Hematological and biochemical responses to three doses of caffeine during the CrossFit® workout: a randomized, double-blind, crossover trial.
content.abstract:
Background

This study investigated the effects of three doses of caffeine (CAF) on hematological and biochemical responses during the CrossFit® workout, a protocol known to induce significant physiological fluctuations.

Methods

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo (PLA)-controlled crossover trial, 26 moderately trained CrossFit® athletes received acute doses of 3, 6, or 9 mgCAF/kgbody mass (BM), or a PLA, 70 min before a 17-min CrossFit® workout.

Results

While exercise was the predominant driver of hematological changes, with no CAF-specific modulation of blood cell indices, significant treatment × time point interactions were observed solely for glucose concentration. Specifically, MEDIUM (6 mgCAF/kgBM) and HIGH (9 mgCAF/kgBM) CAF doses produced significantly greater post-exercise glucose elevations compared to baseline and PLA visits. Phosphates concentrations increased over time, particularly post-exercise, with no treatment effect retained after excluding baseline visit in the sensitivity analysis. Calcium level dynamics were influenced by temporal factors rather than CAF, and magnesium concentration remained stable.

Conclusions

These findings suggest that acute CAF ingestion selectively influences post-exercise glucose responses during the CrossFit® workout, whereas hematological variables and most biochemical markers remain unaffected. Significant post-exercise glucose elevations were observed following the 6 and 9 mgCAF/kgBM conditions compared with baseline and PLA visits, while serum mineral concentrations remained largely stable across treatments.

Clinical trials registration

NCT03822663.

records.title: Novel creatine formulation exhibits similar serum creatine concentrations and pharmacokinetics to creatine monohydrate in healthy adults.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Novel creatine formulation exhibits similar serum creatine concentrations and pharmacokinetics to creatine monohydrate in healthy adults.
content.abstract:
Background

Creatine monohydrate (CrM) is the most widely studied creatine form, demonstrating robust efficacy, bioavailability, and safety. With creatine growing in popularity, alternative formulations of creatine have been developed to target solubility and to optimize absorption pharmacokinetics (PK), as well as to reduce gastrointestinal (GI) intolerability. The purpose of the current study was to evaluate the acute effects of a novel creatine monohydrate (OptiCreatineTM; CrO) compared to CrM on serum creatine PK and GI tolerability in healthy adults.

Methods

Healthy, recreationally active adults (age: 22 ± 3 years; males n = 8, females n = 9) consumed a single 5-gram dose of CrM or CrO across two separate visits following an overnight fast, in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Venous blood samples were collected at baseline and 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, and 300 mins post-ingestion of their assigned treatment to assess serum creatine concentrations. PK parameters including peak concentration (Cmax), time to peak (Tmax), absorption rate constant (ka), elimination rate constant (kel; h-1), and area under the curve (AUC₀-T) were derived using nonlinear regression modeling. GI symptoms were assessed using validated questionnaires.

Results

There was no difference in serum creatine concentrations between CrM or CrO across all participants (p = 0.707), males (p = 0.318), or females (p = 0.996) at any time point. Serum creatine increased over time regardless of treatment (p < 0.0001). No differences were observed between CrM and CrO for Cmax (mean difference ± standard deviation (MD ± SD): 7.66 ± 50.37μM; p = 0.82), Tmax (MD ± SD: -0.04 ± 0.13 h; p = 0.54), ka (MD ± SD: -0.15 ± 0.45 h-1; p = 0.51), kel (MD ± SD: 0.01 ± 0.03 h-1; p = 0.61), or AUC₀-T (MD ± SD: 22.09 ± 160.57 μM·h; p = 0.74), with no sex × treatment interactions (p ≥ 0.05). Descriptive evaluation showed similar GI symptom profiles between conditions, with low frequency and minimal severity reported across both treatments.

Conclusions

A single 5-gram dose of CrO produced similar serum creatine and PK characteristics to CrM in healthy adults. These findings support CrO as a viable delivery option, with no significant differences in acute pharmacokinetic profiles or GI tolerability compared to CrM.

records.title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To investigate the effects of caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg on reactive blocking timing, block-jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses in elite female volleyball players under post-fatigue conditions.

Methods

Fifteen elite female volleyball players completed a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study implemented with double-blinding procedures. Participants consumed placebo (PLA), caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 mg/kg (CAF3) or 6 mg/kg (CAF6), and were tested after supplementation and warm-up at PRE and immediately after a volleyball-specific repeated blocking fatigue protocol (POST). Primary outcomes were reactive blocking timing-chain indices and block-jump (BJ) peak power. Secondary outcomes included additional BJ mechanical variables and general jump measures from countermovement jump (CMJ) and drop jump (DJ) tests. Exploratory outcomes included synchronized surface electromyography (sEMG) variables of lower-limb muscles. Participant blinding was assessed after each visit.

Results

Fatigue impaired jump-related performance across conditions (p < 0.05). For the primary outcomes, the descriptive decline in BJ peak power was 6.9% in CAF6 versus 13.9% in PLA; the adjusted POST comparison did not establish superiority of CAF6 over CAF3. For timing outcomes, overall sequence time increased by 18.4% in PLA, 6.4% in CAF3, and 3.0% in CAF6; CAF6 therefore showed the smallest descriptive deterioration in the integrated sequence measure, whereas CAF3 showed little change in the mean stationary and movement component times. CAF6 showed a reduction in mean stationary response time and the smallest increase in overall sequence time. For secondary outcomes, caffeine showed more favorable post-fatigue responses in selected CMJ/DJ measures, including CMJ mean propulsive power and DJ contact time (p < 0.05), and CAF6 showed greater preservation of selected stretch-shortening cycle-related mechanical measures, including DJ jump height and DJ vertical stiffness, than PLA (p < 0.05). In contrast, CMJ mRSI showed a divergent pattern and was not interpreted as evidence of caffeine-related attenuation of fatigue-induced decrements. Exploratory sEMG results showed smaller post-fatigue changes in selected frequency-domain and activation-timing variables under CAF6, particularly in measures related to extensor-muscle function. Participant masking was incomplete: perceived caffeine ingestion was reported in 0.0%, 53.3%, and 80.0% of PLA, CAF3, and CAF6 visits, respectively, and adverse effects were more frequent in CAF6.

Conclusions

The observed responses were outcome-specific: CAF6 showed a smaller decline in BJ peak power and the smallest increase in overall sequence time, whereas CAF3 showed little change in mean stationary and movement response times. These findings do not establish a generally preferable dose or a timing-stability advantage for CAF3. Incomplete participant masking limits attribution of the differences exclusively to caffeine dose.

records.title: Effects of milk fat globule membrane supplementation on physical function and body composition in older adults: a narrative review.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of milk fat globule membrane supplementation on physical function and body composition in older adults: a narrative review.
content.abstract:
Background

Healthy aging is a priority for many individuals; however, a decline in physical function and poor body composition are common age-related changes that can cause the added years from rising life expectancy to be spent in poor health. Consequently, understanding the mechanisms involved in aging has become increasingly important, including the role of phospholipids (PLs) and how age-related changes in PL content may interfere with lipid metabolism and normal functioning of the musculoskeletal system. Milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) is a bovine milk fraction rich in PLs that may have the potential to support good physical health, so that quality of life can rise alongside life expectancy.

Methods

This narrative review was based on a literature search conducted on Google Scholar, PubMed, and Scopus in May 2026 using the following keywords and Boolean operators: milk fat globule membrane OR MFGM AND physical function OR body composition OR older adults. Studies were included if they were randomized clinical trials (RCTs) investigating MFGM's effects on physical function and/or body composition in older adults.

Results

Findings suggest that MFGM supplementation, when consumed in conjunction with exercise, is an effective way to improve physical function in older adults, particularly among Japanese cohorts; however, changes in habitual diet in response to exercise, variable PL concentrations, and other added ingredients used in interventions may have influenced these results. In contrast, its effects on body composition appear more modest, with some studies reporting no benefits, especially when exercise was not part of the study design, or when compliance may have been a factor.

Conclusions

Beyond the combined use of supplementation and exercise, future RCTs should consistently report participant compliance and, where possible, examine MFGM as a standalone intervention to distinguish its effects from other bioactive ingredients. Greater standardization is also needed, particularly regarding PL dose. Studies should also aim to include participants from more diverse ethnic backgrounds to capture a wider range of physiological responses and improve generalizability of the findings.

records.title: Independent and joint associations of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep with vitamin D status in US adults: a cross-sectional NHANES study.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Independent and joint associations of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep with vitamin D status in US adults: a cross-sectional NHANES study.
content.abstract:
Background

Emerging evidence links movement behaviors to vitamin D status. This study investigated associations between physical activity (PA), sedentary behavior (SB), and sleep with vitamin D status and explored sex differences in these relationships.

Methods

This cross-sectional study included 3195 adults (49.1 ± 17.1 years, 45.5% males) from the 2021-2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey with complete data. Self-reported PA, SB, and sleep duration were assessed. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was measured using high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Generalized linear and logistic regression models were performed.

Results

SB was negatively associated with vitamin D levels in the whole sample (β = -0.006; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.012, -0.001) and males (β = -0.008; 95% CI: -0.014, -0.002), but not females. Sleep duration was positively associated with vitamin D among males only (β = 0.023; 95% CI: 0.003, 0.043). Meeting both PA and SB guidelines showed the strongest and most consistent association with vitamin D sufficiency, observed across the whole sample (odds ratio [OR] = 2.129; 95% CI: 1.504, 3.012), males (OR = 2.013; 95% CI: 1.021, 3.967), and females (OR = 2.214; 95% CI: 1.360, 3.605).

Conclusions

Movement behaviors demonstrate independent and joint associations with vitamin D status in US adults, with modest sex-specific patterns that warrant replication. Combined adherence to PA and SB guidelines was consistently associated with greater odds of vitamin D sufficiency across sexes.

records.title: Feasibility of Heart Rate-Based Total Daily Energy Expenditure Estimation of Pararescuemen in Garrison.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Feasibility of Heart Rate-Based Total Daily Energy Expenditure Estimation of Pararescuemen in Garrison.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Hammond, KG, Bair, AC, Strang, AJ, Young, JC, Kruskall, LJ, Dunnick, DD, and Schilling, BK. Feasibility of heart rate-based total daily energy expenditure estimation of pararescuemen in garrison. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Pararescuemen are a group of Air Force Special Operations Forces who engage in vigorous daily training to prepare for deployment operations. This training can elicit high-energy expenditure, yet few studies have measured the energy expenditure of these airmen while at their home station (in garrison). Twelve operational pararescuemen (age: 27 ± 3 years; years of service: 5 ± 3 years) were assessed for resting energy expenditure, heart rate (HR) at rest and during initial exercise, and the HR-oxygen consumption (V̇o2) linear equation. Subjects' HR was recorded over 2 normal training days and used to estimate total daily energy expenditure (TDEE). Subjects reported an average 9 ± 2 hours of sleep per night of analysis and had an average basal metabolic rate = 82 ± 4 kcal·h-1. Average TDEE was 4,021 ± 890 kcals. Pararescuemen expend high levels of energy during routine training at their home station, similar to those of other elite military groups. Observed and reported high-energy expenditures in pararescuemen suggest further investigation into energy intake in this population to optimize performance.

records.title: Dimensionality Reduction of Full-Body Strength-Power Metrics to Identify Distinct Strength Domains in Elite Rugby Union Athletes.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Dimensionality Reduction of Full-Body Strength-Power Metrics to Identify Distinct Strength Domains in Elite Rugby Union Athletes.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Payne, LKD, Varley, MC, Carey, DL, Driller, MW, and James, LP. Dimensionality reduction of full-body strength-power metrics to identify distinct strength domains in elite rugby union athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to determine the extent of shared and unique information among strength tests and to evaluate whether factors identified through exploratory factor analysis reflect distinct strength domains in professional rugby union players. Twenty professional male rugby union athletes (age 24.4 ± 3.8 years; height 186.3 ± 5.2 cm; body mass 107.6 ± 10.9 kg) completed a battery of 4 upper-body and 5 lower-body isometric, dynamic, and reactive strength tests. A total of 18 metrics were entered into exploratory factor analysis to identify distinct strength domains. Exploratory factor analysis reduced the data set into 2 upper-body domains (pressing and pulling) and 4 lower-body domains (isometric, dynamic, reactive, and relative). These domains together explained 73% of the variance in the upper-body data and 79% of the variance in the lower-body data. The isometric domain was driven by early-phase force at 100 and 200 ms, while peak force contributed less strongly. The dynamic domain was defined by heavy squat velocity, which diverged inversely from countermovement jump height, reflecting load-velocity differences. The reactive domain was shaped by contact time and countermovement depth, highlighting the role of temporal mechanics. The relative domain was defined by drop jump height and countermovement jump momentum, emphasizing the influence of body mass on ballistic force expression. Eighteen test metrics were successfully reduced to 6 distinct domains of strength in professional rugby union athletes. This framework provides a concise basis for profiling upper-body and lower-body strength to reduce redundancy and retain key information needed for training and monitoring rugby athletes.

records.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Benitez, B, Kwak, M, Succi, PJ, Mitchinson, CJ, Snell, ER, and Bergstrom, HC. Gotta go fast: Intended concentric effort produces divergent myoelectric spectral profiles during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine how intended concentric velocity, that is, the volitional effort applied to accelerate a load, influences the spectral characteristics of the surface electromyographic (sEMG) signal during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. Twenty recreationally active adults (10 men and 10 women) performed unilateral leg extensions to task failure at 70% 1 repetition maximum under 2 within-participant conditions as follows: maximal intended concentric velocity (Vmax) and 50% of individualized Vmax (50%Vmax). Bipolar sEMG from the vastus lateralis was decomposed into 10 frequency bands using wavelet-based time-frequency analysis. Band-specific spectral intensities were modeled with a lognormal generalized linear mixed-effects model, and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (ρc) was computed between condition-specific spectral profiles across pairwise time points. The mean propulsive concentric velocity and total repetitions to task failure were secondary outcomes. Significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. The 3-way interaction of condition × frequency × repetition was significant (χ2(3) = 23.98, p < 0.001). Across the set, Vmax redistributed spectral power bidirectionally, increasing the low bands while suppressing the high bands, whereas 50%Vmax increased across the entire spectrum without high-frequency suppression. Despite these divergent profiles, the conditions converged at task failure (ρc = 0.98), and the convergence was asymmetric. The fatigued 50%Vmax profile approximated the fresh Vmax profile (ρc = 0.97) rather than the reverse (ρc = 0.74), indicating that submaximal effort approached the maximal-effort state as fatigue accumulated. The mean propulsive concentric velocity also declined 3.6 times more steeply under Vmax despite similar repetitions. Intended concentric velocity appears to shape the spectral profile of muscle excitation under fixed loading.

records.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness as Mediator in the Association Between Physical Activity and Health-Related Quality of Life in Patients with CMD or OA.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness as Mediator in the Association Between Physical Activity and Health-Related Quality of Life in Patients with CMD or OA.
content.abstract:
